**The father declared his own son's death.** That is the first hard record of this household in Italy, and it carries four things the archive did not have: **Filomena Annecchino named in a document**; **Carminantonio at thirty-six, corroborating a birth in 1901** for the first time; **a son, ANIELLO, born at Forchia about November 1936 and dead at nine months**, who had existed only as a name on the tree; and **an address — Contrada Case Sparse 68**. 

**Two things are deliberately NOT claimed.** A **Maria Annunziata Falco** died at Forchia on 31 July 1938 with her mother indexed as *Filomena Annecchino* and her father as *«Antonio»* — either another child of this house with the father's name written short, or a different couple. **The act has not been read.** And a **Raffaele Falco born at Arpaia married at Forchia on 28 October 1937**; whose son he is has not been established. 

This archive has been caught before treating a name plus a date as an identification. It is not doing it twice in one day.

what: the Sant'Agnese doubt — raised this morning, withdrawn tonight, and the original claim was right
was: Finding generation four's **civil** marriage act at **San Felice a Cancello**, with the bride «*nata in questo Comune, domiciliata in detto comune*», this archive flagged its own published statement that **Sant'Agnese is one of Arienzo's three parishes**. The reasoning was that the bride was the celebrant's own parishioner and appeared to live at San Felice, so his church probably did too — and that the parish act had been read off an **Arienzo film**, which is not the same thing as an Arienzo church.
now: **The act names the place itself.** Read tonight: «*Anno Domini **1844, die 5 mensis Martii** … coram me infrascripto **Parocho S. AGNETIS TERRÆ ARGENTII**, et coram testibus **Pasquale Pellone filio Clementis**, **Angelo di Marzo filio Francisci** … matrimonium contraxerunt in faciem Ecclesiæ per verba de præsenti **RAPHAEL FALCO filius VINCENTII et ANDREANÆ CRISCI**, Archipresbyteralis Ecclesiæ S. Andreæ Apostoli, **et mea Parochiana ANGELA ROSA MORGILLO filia HORATII et VINCENTIÆ PESCE***».\n\n**«TERRA ARGENTI» IS ARIENZO** — and the proof is this archive's own corpus, which uses the phrase over a thousand times in the formula «*Insignis Collegiatae Ecclesiae **Sancti Andreae Apostoli TERRÆ ARGENTI***». Sant'Andrea is Arienzo's collegiate church. **Sant'Agnese is an Arienzo parish, the original claim stands, and the doubt is withdrawn.**
how: Reading the act's own words instead of arguing from where a film was catalogued or where a civil clerk recorded a domicile.
why:
**The flag was still right to raise.** A film label covers a whole reel, this archive has already flip-flopped once between Arienzo and San Felice for exactly that reason, and the civil act genuinely did place the bride at San Felice. **Flagging a claim you cannot presently defend costs a day; asserting one you cannot defend costs the reader's trust.** 

**Two things are corrected in passing.** The witness this archive read as «Eusebio Lettieri di Clemente» is **PASQUALE PELLONE di Clemente** — and the civil act at San Felice names **the same two men**, which is the strongest cross-check the two records could give each other. And **the 5 March date is now read from the act**, so the **four-day gap** with the civil column's «celebration followed on 9 March» is a real disagreement between two books, not a misreading. 

**What remains genuinely odd** is the bride: she is «*mea Parochiana*» of Sant'Agnese **in Arienzo**, while her civil act three days later calls her *domiciled at San Felice*. Both are read from images. **The archive records the tension and does not resolve it.**

what: Filomena Annecchino's birth — tested properly at last, and the premise itself is now in question
was: Twice today this archive gave a reason why her 10 April 1897 birth act has never been found, and **both were guesses about a source rather than tests of it**. First: «the volume is not online, no amount of searching was ever going to find it». Then, pulling that back: «FamilySearch is a separate filming and reaches 1897, so the old paging-and-fuzzy-matching explanation is not refuted».
now: **Tested.** FamilySearch's Benevento collection **does** cover Forchia in 1897 — a control search on **IULIANO**, a common Forchia surname, returns about thirty Forchia records in every year from 1894 to 1899. **And she is still not there.** Searching by her parents — **father Carmine Annecchino, mother Maria Carfora** — returns their children at Forchia: **Giacinta 1883, Agata 1884, Giacomo 1887, Agata 1889, Lucia and Alfonso both 2 August 1892, Alfonso Carmine 1894, Giacomo 1901**. **No child of 1897 among them.** Searching by name for a Filomena Annecchino born 1895–1899 returns **nothing**.
how: A control search first, to prove the source covers the town and the year, and only then a search for the person. **That is the step both earlier explanations skipped.**
why:
**Two possibilities remain and the archive is not choosing.** Either the act exists and is unindexed or misindexed — Antenati holds no Forchia 1897 birth volume at all, so only FamilySearch could have it. **Or she was not born at Forchia in 1897.** 

**That second one this archive has not been willing to say before, and it should be.** The date and the place come from the family tree. **Every one of her supposed siblings is indexed and she alone is not** — which is exactly the shape of a wrong premise rather than a missing page. 

So the next move is **not another search of Forchia**. It is a test of the premise: the neighbouring comuni, Benevento city, and above all **her MARRIAGE to Carminantonio Falco**, which would state her age and birthplace on a record's authority instead of a tree's.

superseded.what: Filomena Annecchino's birth at Forchia in 1897 — the ANSWER WAS ALREADY IN THIS ARCHIVE, and the open question was stale
superseded.note: **She was born at Forchia in 1897.** The second possibility this entry raised — that the premise was wrong — was **withdrawable from a file already in this repository**, `data/qld-bdm.tsv`, which carries her Queensland death registration giving 1897 and her father Carmine. The act is missing; the birth is not.

what: an absence is only evidence when the source would otherwise have shown the thing
was: Two birth acts this archive cannot find: **ANGELO ZAMPIELLO**, born Arpaia 31 August 1895, and **FILOMENA ANNECCHINO**, born Forchia 10 April 1897. Both have been treated the same way for months — as volumes that happen not to be digitised.
now: **They are not the same, and counting what the source holds around them shows it.** Antenati's name index for **ARPAIA** is thin everywhere — births per year 1885–1905 run 4, 2, 4, 2, 4, 1, 0, 3, 2, **0**, **0**, 1, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0. **Angelo's absence explains itself.** The index for **FORCHIA** is the opposite: Carmine Annecchino and Maria Carfora's children are all there — 1883, 1884, 1887, 1889, 1892 twice, 1894, 1901 — **and Filomena alone is missing from a series that holds every one of her siblings.**
how: Running Antenati's **name** index (`/search-nominative/`, which gives parents) on Arpaia for the first time: **259 Zampiello records, 1862–1940**.
why:
**So the two silences mean opposite things.** For Angelo the source is at fault and the family's account stands. For Filomena the source is not at fault, and **what should be doubted is the premise** — the 1897 Forchia birth that comes from the family tree. 

**The rule this archive takes from it:** before treating an absence as a fact about the world, **count what the source holds around it**. A gap in a dense series is a finding; a gap in a sparse one is nothing at all. 

The Arpaia harvest also turned up **TOMMASO ZAMPIELLO × ROSA CRISCI**, whose son Francesco Maria was born there on 29 January 1892. Angelo is «*di Tommaso*». **If it is the same Tommaso, Angelo's mother was Rosa Crisci — and that is not claimed**, because one index entry is not a household and Tommaso is not a rare name at Arpaia.

what: a second child of generation seven — and my own misreading of the act that proves it
was: An index entry showed a **Maria Annunziata Falco** dying at Forchia on 31 July 1938 with mother *Filomena Annecchino* and father *«Antonio»*. This archive flagged it and refused to claim it. Then, reading a contact sheet, **I said the index had the parents wrong** — that the act gave «*Angelo … Annecchino Anna … d'anni trentadue … moglie di Annecchino Gabriele*».
now: **None of that is in the act.** I was reading a **neighbouring entry on the facing page**. Rendered on its own, the act says exactly what the index said: «*… in detto **Ospedale Pellegrini** [Napoli, Montecalvario] **è morta FALCO MARIA ANNUNZIATA di ANTONIO e di ANNECCHINO FILOMENA, di anni CINQUE, da FORCHIA***», at **ten at night on 31 July 1938**, copied back to Forchia at that comune's request on 3 April 1939.
how: Rendering the entry by itself before writing anything down — which is the step that was skipped.
why:
**This archive has published this exact failure before**, in almost these words: *«reading a horizontal band of a register page is not reading an entry — anchor on the margin label and the entry's own first and last words.»* It happened again today, on the first pass. 

**And the act itself is a hard one.** She is **five years old**, of Forchia, born about 1933, and her mother is **Filomena Annecchino** — the exact pairing already documented in this family, whose household Carminantonio is recorded in at Forchia in **August 1937**, declaring the death of their **nine-month-old son Aniello**. **If she is theirs, they buried two children in eleven months**, and the second died in a hospital forty kilometres from home. 

**It is entered as PROBABLE, not documented**: the act writes the father **«Antonio»**, not Carminantonio. It is a Naples act taken from a hospital notice, so a shortening is easy — but it is a different word, and a name plus a date is not an identification.

what: a seventh child for generation six — and two Raffaele Falco where the archive carried one
was: Raffaele Falco and Costanza Maione's children were listed as **Giovanna (1898), Carminantonio (1901), Anna del Giudice (1904), Gerardo (1913)**, with **Giacoma** and **Aniello** undated. Separately the archive says «Carminantonio's son **Raffaele** reached Brisbane, married **Caterina Zampiello** and is buried at Nudgee».
now: **Forchia, marriages 1937, atto 12**, read from the image: on **28 October 1937** at a quarter past six in the morning, in the parish of **San Nicola di Mira**, «***FALCO RAFFAELE**, di anni **ventuno**, contadino, **nato in ARPAIA**, residente in Forchia, **figlio di RAFFAELE e di MAIONE COSTANZA***» married «***CRISCI FRANCESCA**, contadina, figlia di **Pio** e di **De Lucia Maria***». **That is a seventh child of generation six**, born at Arpaia about 1916 — and his father was living at Forchia in 1937, aged about sixty-four.
how: Antenati's name index pointed at the volume; the act was then read leaf by leaf.
why:
**It separates two men the archive had been carrying as one name.** The groom of 1937 is **Carminantonio's BROTHER**, not his son: he is twenty-one, born at Arpaia, and the act names his parents outright. The Brisbane Raffaele who married a **Zampiello** is a different man a generation down. **Two Raffaele Falco in consecutive generations**, and only one of them was on the page. 

**And it puts a second pin in the migration.** Gerardo was born at **Arpaia in 1913** — long called here «the first sign of the move north». A brother born at **Arpaia about 1916** holds the household there for at least three years before it surfaces at **Forchia** in the thirties. **Arienzo → Arpaia → Forchia** now has records at all three. 

**Left unread:** the bride's birthplace is written «**Arienzo S. Felice**», a form that recurs in the same volume. Whether that is a frazione of Arienzo or the clerk's San Felice a Cancello is not settled.

what: Matteo Falco's marriage is not in the Arienzo film — and we may have been searching the wrong town all along
was: The line's oldest question. A Neapolitan marriage act names **both fathers**, so Matteo Falco's own marriage — expected about **1760–66** — is the one record that would push this family above him. It has been hunted in FamilySearch's Arienzo marriage collection for months.
now: **Enumerated rather than searched, and it is not there.** Every marriage act carries the word «*denunciationibus*»; that word returns **515 pages** in the collection, of which **500 were harvested** and read by machine transcript. **The 1760s are densely covered** — 1760:19, 1761:19, 1762:36, 1763:20, 1764:6, 1765:17, 1766:21, 1767:25 — **and not one of those 500 pages carries a legible «Falco» with a year between 1750 and 1779.** The one apparent hit dissolved on reading: the «alco» was OCR debris for *aliis*, and the page is **1865**, not 1765. **The earliest Falco marriage page in the whole harvest is 1782.**
how: Enumerating the collection on a word every act of that type carries, instead of searching for names the machine renders as *Marteus Falco*, *Armeni Falco* and *Malco*.
why:
**The negative is bounded and stated as such**: the surname may have been lost by the OCR, or the act may sit on one of the fifteen pages not harvested. **But the useful outcome is not the negative — it is that we may have been reading the wrong town.** 

**Today this archive learned where a marriage is recorded.** Generation four's civil act was hunted through sixty-four consecutive Arienzo acts of 1843–44 and was not there, because **the promise is made in the BRIDE's comune** — San Felice a Cancello. The same rule governs the church: a couple marries in **the bride's parish**, which is precisely why Raffaele Falco of Sant'Andrea married at **Sant'Agnese**, «*mea Parochiana*». 

**Matteo is certainly at Arienzo** — he witnesses a marriage there in **1759**, before his own. **Francesca Crisci need not have been.** If she was not an Arienzo parishioner, her marriage is in her own town's book and no amount of reading Arienzo will ever find it. 

**So the next move is to find HER**: a Crisci baptism of about 1740–45 outside Arienzo, and the Crisci of San Felice a Cancello, Santa Maria a Vico, Arpaia, Forchia and Cervino.

superseded.what: WHERE MATTEO FALCO'S MARRIAGE IS NOT — swept through the BRIDE's surname, and this time the denominator is honest
superseded.note: **Re-swept through the BRIDE's surname**, which is the cleaner instrument: 1,277 pages under CRISCI, ninety-two per cent of them Arienzo, regexed locally so the negative no longer depends on the engine spelling *Falco* correctly. **Still not a nil** — the 1750s and 1760s are thin, and eighteenth-century years are written in Latin words that no digit count sees.

what: Maria Carfora's parents are not reachable through Antenati — three routes, all shut
was: The descent of **Filomena Annecchino** from **Carmine Annecchino and Maria Carfora** is *inferred, not documented*. One act naming **Maria Carfora's own parents** would settle it, and Antenati's name index — which gives parents — had never been run on the Carfora.
now: **Run: 260 Carfora records at Forchia, 190 births, 59 deaths, 11 marriages.** She is in it, and **only ever as somebody's mother** — «*Maria Carfora, Figlio = Giacinta Annecchino · Agata Annecchino · Alfonso Carmine Annecchino*» — with **no birth date, no place and no parents of her own** on any row.
how: Harvesting the whole surname for the town and reading every death act in it, rather than searching for her by name.
why:
**Three routes and all three are shut, which is worth writing down so nobody walks them again.** 

**Her own birth act** is not linked, and Forchia offers too many candidates in the window — Maria Antonia 1861, Maria Filomena 1863, Maria Sabata 1863, Maria Carmina 1863, Maria Grazia 1865, Maria Francesca 1866, Maria Giovanna 1867 and 1869 — **with nothing to choose between them.** 

**Her marriage**, about 1880–82, falls **inside the Forchia gap**: Antenati's marriages there run 1809–1865, then 1931–1941, and nothing between. 

**Her death** is not in the indexed window: **all 59 Carfora death acts were read and not one has an Annecchino spouse.** 

**What the harvest gave instead** is the Carfora of Forchia as households rather than names — Carmine × Raffaela Crisci, Antonio × Maria Papa, Gabriele × Lucia Crisci, Michele × Maria Rosa Fusco, Agostino × Porzia D'Ambrosio and six more. **And two of them were born at ARIENZO and died at Forchia.** The Carfora were walking the **same corridor as the Falco**, a generation or two earlier. No kinship is claimed; **it is the road that is the point, not the blood.**

what: the processetti of Caserta do not hold generation seven's marriage either
was: **Carminantonio Falco × Filomena Annecchino's marriage** is the cleanest available test of whether she was really born at Forchia in 1897 — a marriage act states the bride's age and birthplace on a record's authority rather than a tree's. It has never been found.
now: **Collection 2043630 turns out to be THE PROCESSETTI** — «Marriage Supplement», «Marriage Proclamation», «Marriage Bann Supplement» for the Caserta comuni, **1866–1929**, with **1,503 Falco pages**. A marriage dossier copies out the bride's **birth extract in full**, so this was the best remaining hope. **They are not in it.** Searching the collection for Falco-and-Annecchino returns three pages, all from **Castel Campagnano** — a Di Carlo × Falco marriage with an unrelated Rosa Annecchino.
how: Reading what the collection actually is before mining it. It had been recorded here only as «Caserta SMCV Tribunale, 1,503 Falco pages», which says nothing about what kind of record it holds.
why:
**The negative places the marriage rather than just failing to find it.** This is a **CASERTA** collection. If the couple had married in a Caserta comune — Arienzo above all — the dossier would be here. It is not, which points at **Forchia or Arpaia**, both **Benevento**. 

**And Forchia's marriages run 1809–1865 and then 1931–1941.** Their marriage, before 1930, falls in that gap, as does **Carmine Annecchino × Maria Carfora's** of about 1880. **Two marriages this family needs are in the same twenty-five-year hole**, and it is a hole in the filming, not in the records. 

That is now written down on the new [Holdings](/holdings) page, with every other gap this archive has had to discover by hand.

what: Vincenzo Falco's death is not in the Arienzo parish register — all 703 Falco pages read
was: Generation three. **VINCENZO FALCO**, baptised 1 February 1792, married Andreana Crisci in December 1814 — and, as of today, **alive on strada Cammellara on 7 March 1844**, named in his son's marriage act with no *quondam* before him. The Arienzo civil death registers are read act by act to **1858** and he is not in them. His death has never been found.
now: **The parish death register has now been enumerated for him and he is not there either.** FamilySearch's Arienzo deaths collection (`M9J1-SMK`, **1733–1888**) returns **703 pages** mentioning a Falco; **all 703 were harvested** and their transcripts searched for a *Vincenzo* standing within thirty characters of a *Falco* anywhere near a death verb. **Two hits, and both dissolve**: a «Cav. Vincenzo De Falco», a registrar at **Pomigliano** in 1926, and a «Falcone Vincenzo» — a different surname at a different comune.
how: Paging the whole result set rather than sampling it, and testing proximity rather than mere co-occurrence: in a town this size, «Vincenzo» and «Falco» appear on the same page constantly without belonging to the same man.
why:
**The negative is bounded, and the boundaries matter more than the result.** The machine's Latin is bad — it renders this family as *Marteus Falco*, *Armeni Falco*, *Salco*, *Malco* — so a mangled «Vincentius Falco» could have slipped past. And **the collection stops at 1888**: if he outlived that, it was never going to hold him. 

**What is left is the civil series.** Antenati's Arienzo death registers run on past 1858 and **have never been read after it**. That is now the only untried route, and it is a reading job, not a search. 

He was **fifty-two** in March 1844 and his own father Pasquale reached sixty-seven, so a death anywhere from the 1850s to the 1870s is unremarkable — **which is exactly why the unread volumes are the place to look.**

superseded.what: Arienzo deaths 1859 read from the year's own index — and the series stops at 1865
superseded.note: **The remaining route is bounded, not open-ended.** Antenati holds 57 Arienzo death volumes and they stop at **1865** — so the civil series after 1858 is **seven years long**, of which 1859 is now read out and holds no Vincenzo.

what: generation six's marriage dossier, opened — and it documents the line a generation deeper
was: Collection 2043630 was recorded here as «Caserta SMCV Tribunale, 1,503 Falco pages» — a description that says nothing about what kind of record it holds, and it had never been mined. Generation six's marriage was known only as a date on a family tree.
now:
**It is the PROCESSETTI**, and generation six's fascicolo is open: **«1897 — Registro dei Matrimoni — FALCO RAFFAELE · MAIONE COSTANZA — Numero 41, Parte 1ª — DOCUMENTI INCLUSI N. SEI»**, with banns published on **12 and 19 September 1897**.

**The groom's birth extract** — 1873, act 39 — reads: «*è comparso **CARMINANTONIO FALCO di Raffaele, contadino, di anni VENTIDUE**, domiciliato in Arienzo, **VIA DEGLI ORTI** … un bambino … **nato il giorno SEI corrente mese di Aprile ad ore ventidue** dalla di lui moglie **GIOVANNA ARRICALE FU FRANCESCO** … dichiara di dare il nome di **RAFFAELE***».

**The certificate of poverty** reads: «*Il Sindaco certifica che **FALCO RAFFAELE di CARMINANTONIO** e **MAIONE COSTANZA DI ANIELLO**, nati e domiciliati in questo Comune, **SONO POVERI*** — Arienzo, 29 Agosto 1897».
how: Reading what a collection IS before mining it, then searching it for the couple rather than for the surname.
why:
**Four things this archive did not have.** Generation six's birth date **confirmed from the act**. Generation five **corroborated independently** — his father is twenty-two in April 1873, so born about 1850–51, against a recorded 10 July 1850. **GIOVANNA ARRICALE's own father, Francesco**, named for the first time, and her surname spelt **Arricale** rather than *Arricole*. And **an address: VIA DEGLI ORTI** — so generation five had **moved off strada Camellara**, which four generations before them never did. 

**And they married as paupers.** The dossier was drawn free because the sindaco certified them poor. That is not a detail the tree could ever have carried. 

**Bound a few leaves away — and NOT part of their fascicolo** — is a death extract of **1883, act 60: PASQUALE FALCO, 44, agricoltore, died at VIA CAMELLARA NUMBER FIVE on 26 September 1883, «del fu FRANCESCO e della fu RAFFAELA FALCO», husband of MARIA AMALIA GUIDA.** That is the Francesco × Raffaela household, it gives them **a son the archive did not have**, and it is **the first house number ever recovered for strada Camellara.** The attribution is stated plainly: it was found because the volume is searchable, not because it belongs to this couple.

what: a daughter for generation five, and both of Costanza Maione's parents
was: Generation five's children were known only through **Raffaele**, generation six. **Costanza Maione's parents were unknown** — the Maione page said hers was «the one wife's birth in the spine with a record behind it», and that record named no father or mother.
now:
**Two publication acts from the same collection settle both.**

**26 August 1897:** «*è comparso **FALCO RAFFAELE, di anni VENTIQUATTRO** … **figlio di CARMINANTONIO, di anni QUARANTASEI** … e di **GIOVANNA ARRICALE** … E pure comparsa: **MAIONE COSTANZA, di anni VENTUNO** … **figlia di ANIELLO, di anni CINQUANTASEI**, contadino … **e figlia di MARTONE ANNA**, contadina*». **Costanza Maione was the daughter of ANIELLO MAIONE, born about 1841, and ANNA MARTONE**, both living at Arienzo.

**24 August 1902:** «*E pure comparsa: **FALCO ANGELA ROSA, di anni VENTIDUE**, contadina, **figlia di CARMINANTONIO** … **e figlia di ARRICALE GIOVANNA***», marrying **FRANCESCO ESPOSITO**, 26, colono of **San Felice a Cancello**, son of Paolo and the late **Marta Morgillo**. **A daughter of generation five, born about 1880, that this archive did not have.**
how: Reading the marriage publications in collection 2043630 — the same volumes as the processetti — for the couple rather than for the surname.
why:
**She was named ANGELA ROSA for her grandmother** — Angela Rosa Morgillo, generation four's wife, who died in **April 1880**, about when this child was born. The naming-after-the-dead that this archive has documented in Latin for the 1770s is still running in **1880**, in living memory. 

**And her husband's mother was a MORGILLO of San Felice a Cancello** — which is precisely what generation four's wife was. **No kinship is claimed.** Two generations on, the same two families were still moving in the same small orbit between Arienzo and San Felice. 

**One discrepancy is published rather than smoothed.** Carminantonio's age is **forty-six** in August 1897 and **fifty-five** in August 1902 — nine years of ageing in five. The Arienzo clerks guessed, as this archive has shown before; his recorded birth of **10 July 1850** sits between the two.

what: Arienzo deaths 1859 read from the year's own index — and the series stops at 1865
was: The named next step for **generation three**: Antenati's Arienzo civil death registers **after 1858**, never read. **Vincenzo Falco** is alive on strada Cammellara on 7 March 1844 and is in neither the 1844–58 civil sweep nor — as of yesterday — the parish register's 703 Falco pages.
now: **Two things before a single act was opened.** Antenati holds **57 Arienzo death volumes and they run 1809–1865**: there are **no post-1865 Arienzo civil deaths on Antenati at all**, so this route is **seven years long**, not open-ended. And **the 1859 volume opens with a TAVOLA ALFABETICA** — an alphabetical table of the year's dead giving act number, name, profession, **the parents' names** and the date. **One page instead of sixty-eight.**\n\n**The complete F section for 1859:** act 19, **FALCO MARIA**, contadina, of **Michele and d'Ambrogio Giovanna**, died **4 March**; act 55, **FALCO CARMELA**, of **Michele and Vigliotto Antonia**, died **4 August**; act 60, **FALCO RAFFAELE**, of **Michele and d'Ambrogio Maria Giovanna**, died **17 August**. **No Vincenzo. 1859 is eliminated.**
how: Reading the year's own index rather than the year's acts — and checking, first, how far the series actually runs.
why: **Three children fall out of it for two households the archive already had, and both gain a generation of detail.** **Michele Falco × Maria Giovanna d'Ambrosio** was known only by «a daughter Antonia born 19 November 1850»; it now has **Maria** and **Raffaele**. **Michele Falco × Antonia Vigliotta** was known only by «a daughter Chiara who died in 1846 aged seven»; it now has **Carmela**. **Neither household is claimed as kin** — they are recorded so the next Falco found at Arienzo can be checked against them. \n\n**And a method note that will save a day later: the tavola moves.** 1859 has its index at the **front**; **1860 does not** — that volume runs straight into the acts and was still running at image 58 of 60. The archive has already recorded a «tavola bound at the front» for 1850. **Check both ends of every volume before concluding there is no index.**

what: Moiano tested as Filomena Annecchino's real birthplace — and it fails
was: Filomena Annecchino's birth act of **10 April 1897 at Forchia** cannot be found, and her siblings are all indexed while she alone is not. This archive said the premise itself should be doubted — **that she may not have been born at Forchia at all** — and named **MOIANO**, the Annecchino's other stronghold, as the place to test.
now: **Tested, and it fails.** Antenati's name index for Moiano holds **215 Annecchino, 1861–1942** — 158 births, 48 deaths, 12 marriages — resolving into **fifteen distinct households**. They marry **Cuozzo, Saccone, Morzillo, Di Stasi, Cieri, Mauriello, Perna**. **Not one Carfora. Not one Crisci.** Moiano's own Filomena Annecchino married a **Ruggiero** and bore children from **1879**, so she is a generation too early and the wrong family.
how: Harvesting the whole surname for the town and resolving it into households, instead of searching for one name in it.
why:
**The Moiano and Forchia Annecchino are distinct groups** — the same surname, eight kilometres apart, marrying entirely different families. **So the hypothesis this archive raised against itself does not hold**, and **Carmine Annecchino × Maria Carfora of Forchia remain the best fit** for her parents. 

**That leaves the question exactly where it was, which is the honest outcome**: her act is not indexed by either institution, her siblings all are, and the reason is still unknown. **What has been ruled out is the explanation this archive itself proposed.** 

It cost one harvest to find out, and the 215 records are kept — fifteen Annecchino households of Moiano that nobody had looked at.

superseded.what: Filomena Annecchino's birth at Forchia in 1897 — the ANSWER WAS ALREADY IN THIS ARCHIVE, and the open question was stale
superseded.note: **The question did not stay where it was.** Filomena was born at Forchia in 1897 on this archive's own evidence. The Moiano negative itself stands, and the fifteen Moiano Annecchino households are still worth what they cost.

what: generation five's marriage dossier is outside the filmed range — not missed, not there
was: Having opened generation six's fascicolo of 1897, the obvious next target was **generation five's**: **Carminantonio Falco × Giovanna Arricale**, who must have married about **1870–72** — their son Raffaele was born 6 April 1873 and his father was twenty-two. Collection 2043630 runs **1866–1929**, so it should hold it.
now: **It does not, and it never could.** Five hundred Falco pages were harvested and their year-mentions counted **for Arienzo alone**: 1865:2, **1871:1, 1872:2, 1873:1, 1874:3**, then **1875:19**, 1877:4, 1878:4, 1879:4, 1880:5 … **The series is almost empty before 1875 and dense after.** \n\n**And every one of the seven pre-1875 mentions, read individually, is a birth extract QUOTED INSIDE A LATER DOSSIER** — «*per l'anno 1872 … Maria Carmina Loffredo*», certified «*Arienzo 22 Aprile 1897*»; «*dell'anno 1872 … Perrotta Filomena*», «*Dato ad Arienzo il dì 7 Febbraio 1896*», on a form printed «**(Modulo 1865 al 1874)**»; «*per l'anno 1874 … Morgillo Alessandra*», «*Visto Arienzo 14 Dicembre 1895*». **Not one is a fascicolo of its own.**
how: Counting the collection's year coverage for the town before hunting a document in it — then reading the few early hits individually instead of trusting the histogram.
why:
**The Arienzo allegati in this collection begin about 1875.** Generation five married before that, so their dossier is **outside the filmed range** — not missed, not mis-indexed, simply absent. Generation six's of 1897 sits comfortably inside it, which is why that one opened first time. 

**This is a holdings fact, not a search failure**, and it is now on the Holdings page so the hunt is not repeated. **The remaining route is the Arienzo civil marriage registers themselves for 1870–72**, which Antenati does hold — a reading job, like the deaths after 1858. 

The years 1866–1874 survive in this collection **only as documents copied into marriages of the 1890s** — which is, incidentally, exactly how Raffaele Falco's own 1873 birth extract reached us.

superseded.what: GENERATION FIVE'S MARRIAGE DATE, AND GIOVANNA ARRICALE'S PARENTS — found in the collection an archive note had closed
superseded.note: **The marriage is indexed in that collection after all** — `1:2:HHBF-FZWK`, 18 November 1872 at Arienzo, with **Giovanna Arricale's parents named**. What this entry established about the physical *allegati* being thin before 1875 may still hold; **the note that closed the collection to searching did not.**

what: the processetti mined out — 1,431 pages, four Arienzo Falco acts, and a household documented twice
was: Collection 2043630 holds **1,503 Falco pages** for Arienzo and had been probed but never mined. The hope was that its dossiers, which copy out birth and death extracts in full, would reach the **Arienzo civil deaths after 1865** that Antenati simply does not hold.
now: **1,431 pages harvested and searched. The true yield is four acts**, and saying so plainly is the point: **deaths — 1883 act 60, Pasquale Falco; 1909 act 70, Clementina Falco. Births — 1873 act 39, Raffaele Falco; 1877 act 20, Pasqualina Falco.** Everything else naming a Falco is **another comune or another role**.
how: Harvesting the whole result set, then sorting the extracts **by comune and by the Falco's role in them** before reading any of them as family.
why:
**Most Falco in this collection are registrars, not relatives.** *Giuseppe de Falco, sindaco of **Caserta***, signs birth extracts through the 1860s; *Falco Raffaele, consigliere of **Caivano***, signs deaths in 1903, 1904 and 1907; *Falco Giacomo, assessore of **Sessa Aurunca***, signs in 1900. **Reading the name without reading the role would have produced a dozen false ancestors.** 

**And one household is now documented twice, six years apart.** In February **1877** «*è comparso **PASQUALE FALCO, di anni TRENTOTTO**, contadino … nella casa posta in **VIA CAMELLARA**, da **MARIA AMALIA GUIDA** sua moglie … è nato un bambino di sesso femminile … **PASQUALINA***». In September **1883** «*nella casa posta in **via Camellara al numero cinque**, è morto **PASQUALE FALCO, di anni QUARANTAQUATTRO** … **del fu Francesco e della fu Raffaela Falco**, marito di **Maria Amalia Guida***». **The same man — thirty-eight, then forty-four — born about 1839.** 

So three generations of a collateral household stand on this family's own street: **Francesco × Raffaela → Pasquale × Maria Amalia Guida → Pasqualina**. **A discrepancy is left standing**: the birth gives the house as «numero ventic[inque]», the death as «numero cinque». Either they moved along the street or the machine ate a syllable. 

**A second household too**: **CLEMENTINA FALCO**, born about 1857, **«del fu MATTEO»**, died at **via Orticelli 20** in September 1909 — a **later Matteo Falco of Arienzo**, not the founder who died in 1802, and on the very street generation five lived in. **No kinship claimed.**

what: Don Giovanni Falco's baptism day — read from the act at last
was: The founder's grandson who took orders. The archive had his baptism only as **«April 1825»** — a month with no day, from the machine transcript — and his death, **26 November 1849**, where the act calls him **«DON GIOVANNI FALCO, DIACONO, di anni venticinque»**.
now: **Read from the image** (`3Q9M-CSD3-132V-3`), the margin reading «**Joannes Falco**»: «*Anno Domini **1825** = Die vero **6 APRILIS** = Rev[erendu]s D[ominus] Franciscus de Nuprijs [?] Sub[stitu]tus **baptizavit infantem natum ex JOSEPHO FALCO et ANTONIA DI GUIDA Conjugibus***».
how: Rendering the spread at a low level to find the margin label, then the entry itself — and re-painting the canvas immediately before the capture, because the portal's own page kept repainting over it.
why: **Baptised 6 April 1825, dead 26 November 1849 — twenty-four years and seven months.** His death act rounds it to twenty-five, which is the usual thing and worth noting rather than reconciling. \n\nHe is **the founder's great-grandson** — Matteo Falco → Giuseppe Falco × Antonia di Guida → Giovanni — and **the only man in this family known to have taken orders**, from a household of *contadini* on strada Camellara. The archive has already had to be careful here once: it nearly filed a labourer's son who took orders with the gentry Don Francesco Falco's son who did the same. **This act keeps the two apart by naming his parents outright.**

what: the eldest of Giuseppe Falco's seven, read from the act
was: **GIOVANNA FALCO**, first child of **Giuseppe Falco and Antonia di Guida**, was held on a machine transcript alone — «13 Aug 1805» and two parents, from a page the machine renders as «*Adui Mangiuo di Lula Vardi rio Sabia sus baptizavitinfantennaan e Josepho Falco e Antonio di Guida*».
now: **Read from the image**, margin «**Joanna Falco**»: «*Anno D[omi]ni **1805**, die vero **13 AUGUSTI** … baptizavit infantem natam ex **JOSEPHO FALCO** et **ANTONIA DI GUIDA** Conjugibus **hujus Archipresbyteralis Ecclesiae**, cui dedit nomen **JOANNA**. Matrina fuit **FORTUNATA VILLANO**. **HYACINTHUS Archipresbyter MORGILLO***».
how: Rendering the spread to find the margin, then the entry — two rows down from where the first crop landed, which is why the crop below it turned out to be an Angelo Ruotolo.
why: **The machine had the date right, and nothing else.** The act adds the **godmother, Fortunata Villano**, the **archpriest Giacinto Morgillo** who wrote it, and the plain statement that this household belonged to **the archpresbyteral church** — Sant'Andrea Apostolo, the collegiate church of Arienzo, not one of the lesser parishes. \n\nThat matters because **generation four's own marriage in 1844 turned on exactly this distinction**: the groom belonged to Sant'Andrea and the bride to Sant'Agnese, and they married in hers. **Giuseppe's household is now placed in the same church as his nephew's**, from a document rather than an inference.

what: a ten-day life, and the godmother who links two households on one street
was: **RAFFAELE FALCO**, third child of Giuseppe Falco and Antonia di Guida, was a machine transcript: a date, two parents, and an «obiit» note. The page the machine renders as «*aria Reggier Io Fiaciache e di Morgistel Anno di 1881 Tevero 16 Mari*».
now: **Read from the image**, margin «**Raphael Falco** / **obiit die 26 Februarii 1811**»: «*Anno D[omi]ni **1811**, die vero **16 FEBRUARII** … baptizavit infantem natum ex **JOSEPHO FALCO** et **ANTONIA DI GUIDA** conjugibus **hujus Parochiae**, cui dedit nomen **RAPHAEL**. **Matrina fuit SARA RUGGIERO**. HYACINTHUS Archipresbyter MORGILLO*».
how: Reading the act's own opening line separately — the entry immediately below it is *also* dated 16 February, so taking the date from the neighbour would have looked right and proved nothing.
why:
**He lived ten days.** Baptised on the sixteenth, dead on the twenty-sixth, and the margin of his baptism is where his death is recorded — the same hand, the same page. 

**And the godmother is somebody this archive already knows.** **SARA RUGGIERO** is the wife of **Arcangelo Crisci**, of **strada Camellara** — documented here from the death of their seven-day-old daughter Carmela in January 1815, in an act read during the 1815 sweep. **So in February 1811 she stood godmother to Giuseppe Falco's son.** 

That is the first time this archive has caught **two of its own documented households in the same room**. It claims no kinship: godparenthood is a neighbour's office as often as a relative's — but it is exactly the kind of tie that [a single street](/camellara) produces, and it is evidence of the sort the registers rarely hand over.

what: an aunt at the font — the 1812 baptism ties two of the founder's sons together
was: **FRANCESCA FALCO**, fourth child of Giuseppe Falco and Antonia di Guida, was a machine transcript — a date, two parents, and a page rendered «*Cacharia Rege Agacintin Archipa Morzillo Anno D1812 . Die ugro 27 Ocobris*».
now: **Read from the image**, margin «**Francisca Falco**»: «*Anno D[omi]ni **1812**, die vero **27 OCTOBRIS**, R[everendu]s D[ominu]s **Joannis Crisci** Substitutus … baptizavit infantem natam ex **JOSEPHO FALCO** et **ANTONIA DI GUIDA** Conjugibus hujus Parochiae, cui dedit nomen **FRANCISCA MARIA**; **Matrina fuit VICTORIA CIMMINO***. Hyacinthus Archipresbyter Morgillo».
how: Reading the act's own opening line separately again — the first crop landed on the entry below, an *Alexander delle Cave* of 28 October, and the one above it on a Paulus Porrino.
why:
**The godmother is the child's own aunt.** **VITTORIA CIMMINO** married **GIOACCHINO FALCO** on 16 May 1796 — and Gioacchino and Giuseppe were both sons of **Matteo Falco**, the founder. So at this font in October 1812 stood **one brother's wife holding the other brother's daughter**. 

That is the first time this archive has seen **two of the founder's own children's households meet inside a single act.** Everything before has been inference from shared streets and repeated names; this is the family in one room. 

It also quietly strengthens something the archive had only argued: that **Gioacchino Falco really is Matteo's son**, a claim built until now on a baptism of 1779 and the naming of a dead brother. **Aunts stand godmother; strangers of the same surname do not.**

what: a question this archive had already answered, left standing on the open-questions page for months
was: The open questions page asked **«What became of three daughters?»** — Giovanna, Francesca Maria Lucia and **Maddalena**, children of Giuseppe Falco and Antonia di Guida — and said that none of them appears in the Arienzo death registers of 1844–1858, so they «married, died before 1844, or left».
now: **Maddalena did not need finding. This archive had already buried her.** She died on **31 May 1825**, a week short of her seventh birthday, at strada Camellara — her act is atto 30 of the 1825 death register, declared by Cesare and Francesco Cossi, and it is written up on the *What has been searched* page, where it notes that Giuseppe and Antonia buried two children in nineteen days. The open question named her anyway. It now names **two** daughters, and says why it used to name three.
how: By reading her **baptism** from the image on 14 September 2026 and then doing the thing this archive's own rule requires — checking the find against what is already held **in the same pass**. The check found no new person. It found a contradiction between two of this site's own pages.
why: **This is the failure mode that a fresh find hides.** The baptism was new, correct and worth publishing, and publishing it alone would have left the stale question sitting there. An archive of this size contradicts itself silently: one page learns something and the pages that asked the question never hear. The rule about checking a find against existing holdings is not only a guard against wrong attachments — it is the only routine that catches an answer that never propagated.

what: «no record yet names Antonia's parents» — while the act that names them sat in two of this archive's own data files
was: The surnames page said of **Antonia di Guida**, generation three's wife: «*A man of that age could father both him and Antonia.* **not established** — *no record yet names Antonia's parents.*» It then built a careful, hedged case for the Giuseppe di Guida of strada Maddalena as her likely father.
now: **Her parents are named, in her own marriage act.** Arienzo, **4 August 1802**, the act that also proves Giuseppe Falco to be Matteo's son — read from the image long ago — calls the bride «*filiam **Josephi** e **Magdalenae***». Her father was a Giuseppe di Guida and her mother a Maddalena. The hedge was pointed at the wrong question: what is genuinely open is not *whether a record names her father* but **whether that Giuseppe is the massaro of strada Maddalena**, since the act gives him no street, no age and no trade.
how: By checking a newly-read baptism — Maddalena Falco's, 7 June 1818 — against everything already held for the same household, which is what this archive's rule requires and which turns up its own pages as often as it turns up new people.
why: **A hedge is not automatically honest.** «Not established» reads like caution, and here it was concealing a fact the archive had already recovered and then failed to carry across from a data file to a page. The lesson is the same one the stale open question taught on the same day: **this archive's largest single source of error is now itself** — findings that land in one place and never propagate. Both were caught by the same check, in the same pass, from the same act.

what: the same woman's surname read two different ways off the same act — PIVERA or RIVETTA — SETTLED THE SAME DAY
was: Nothing, publicly. The split was invisible because the two readings live in different files and neither page quoted the other.
now: **The act says RIVETTA.** Re-rendered at magnification on 14 September 2026: «*…et **Antoniam di Guida filiam Josephi, et Magdalenæ RIVETTA**, utrosq̃ meos parochianos, servata forma Ritu: Roma:…*» — double **t**, terminal **-a**. **And the control is inside the same frame**: the very next line carries «*Ritu: Roma:*», two capital **R** from the same pen at the same size, and they match the initial of *Rivetta* exactly. **PIVERA was the OCR, copied into `data/households.tsv` and never checked.** The human reading in `data/arienzo-parish-acts.tsv` was right the whole time.
how: Found by reading the two files side by side while checking Maddalena Falco's baptism against existing holdings. **Then traced to source.** The page's machine transcript reads «*Josephun Falco filium Matthei, e Francisce Crisci e Antonian di Guida filian Josephi e Magdele **PIVERA***» — so the PIVERA in `households.tsv` is **the OCR, copied**, not a second person's look at the handwriting.
why: **The machine was wrong and the archive's own earlier reading was right — and for six hours today this page said neither could be trusted.** That was the correct state to publish while it was true. What made it resolvable was refusing to settle it by plausibility: RIVETTA is this corpus's commonest surname, so adopting it on those grounds would have produced the right answer for a bad reason, and the same move would have produced a wrong one elsewhere. **The test that worked was finding a control letter in the same hand, in the same frame** — here two capital R eight words later. That is now the standard for any single-letter dispute in this archive: don't argue from frequency, find the same scribe writing the same letter nearby.

what: ANTONIA DI GUIDA'S PARENTS, NINE SIBLINGS AND HER OWN BIRTH DATE — proven the same day it was proposed
was: The archive held **two unconnected records**. From the marriage act of 4 August 1802: Antonia di Guida, wife of Giuseppe Falco, was «*filiam Josephi, et Magdalenæ …*» — a father and mother with no street, no age, no trade. Separately, from an Arienzo death act of **21 October 1817**: **Angelo Andrea di Guida**, husband of Teresa Vigliotta, «*figlio di Giuseppe di Guida e **Michedalena Rivetti***». And separately again, from **6 September 1819**: «*Giuseppe di Guida, di anni sessantotto, massaro di campagna, domiciliato in questo comune, **strada Maddalena***» — born about 1751. The surnames page called the link «*a lead*» and declined it.
now: **Reading the 1802 act's mother's surname from the image closed the gap: it is RIVETTA.** So both records name the same pair — **Giuseppe di Guida** and a **Ma(dda)lena Rivetti/Rivetta** — in one small comune, fifteen years apart. The archive had already noticed that «*Michedalena*» is the scribe's own line-break blend and glossed it as a Campanian form of **Maddalena**. On that reading: **Antonia di Guida's parents were Giuseppe di Guida and Maddalena Rivetti of strada Maddalena**, and **Angelo Andrea di Guida was her brother**. **PROVEN, four hours later, by the instrument this entry asked for: a di Guida baptism naming both parents. In fact ten of them.** A sweep of the Arienzo baptism register (1,298 pages) returns **Giuseppe di Guida × Maddalena Rivetta with nine children between 1773 and 1791** — and two of those acts close the case by themselves. **ANTONIA**, «*baptizavit infantem natam ex **Josepho di Guida, et Magdalena Rivetta** … quae nominata est **ANTONIA**. Matrina fuit **Prudentia Papa***» — **read from the image**, «*Anno D̄ni Millesimo Septingentesimo **octogesimo tertio** … die vero **trigesimaprima 31 Octobris***». And **ANGELO ANDREAS**, baptised **29 November 1791** to the same couple — the same man whose civil death act of 21 Oct 1817 names «*Giuseppe di Guida e Michedalena Rivetti*». Parish and civil, independently, on the same household.
how: A full-text sweep of the Arienzo baptisms (collection `M9J1-7MY`, 1,298 distinct pages) for *Guida*, then a regex across the machine transcripts for any *di Guida* standing beside a Rivetta-shaped surname — then **one act read from the image** to fix the year the machine could not render.
why: **Three things this settles at once, and one it deliberately does not.** It gives generation three's wife a **birth date** — **31 October 1783** — so she married at **eighteen** and was **thirty-four**, not «trenta», when Maddalena was born in 1818; the clerks' age-guessing is confirmed again. It confirms **RIVETTA** a third time, in a different scribe's hand nineteen years before the marriage act. And it turns «Michedalena» from a puzzle into a **civil clerk's blend** of a name the parish always wrote *Magdalena*. **What it does not do is pretend the risk was imaginary.** This entry warned that «*nothing yet excludes a second such couple*» — and the same sweep found one: **Filippo di Guida × Margherita Rivetta**, whose daughter Vittoria was baptised 15 February 1779. Two di Guida men married two Rivetta women in one parish. The forenames separate them, and the caution was right to be there.

what: the age the civil clerks gave Antonia di Guida was five years out — and the archive had built a birth year on it
was: The surnames page said «**Antonia di Guida** was thirty when her daughter Maddalena was born on 7 June 1818, **so born about 1788**» — taking the civil clerk's «*d'anni trenta*» at face value.
now: **She was baptised on 31 October 1783**, so she was **thirty-four** in June 1818 and **eighteen** at her marriage in August 1802. The «about 1788» was five years late.
how: Her own baptism, found in a full-text sweep of the Arienzo baptism register and read from the image.
why: **This archive already knew these clerks guessed.** The age series for Giuseppe Falco runs thirty-two, thirty-seven, thirty-six, forty-three, forty-two, forty-two, forty across nine years of acts. Antonia's «trenta» was used anyway, because it was the only figure available — and a figure that is the only one available still is not evidence. **Where a derived birth year rests on a stated age, the page should say so**, and this one now does.

what: a granddaughter called Maddalena — the di Guida reconstruction predicted a name, and the register has it
was: Nothing. Angelo Andrea di Guida was a name in a death act of 21 October 1817 with a widow, Teresa Vigliotta, and «no age, no parents, no children».
now: **He had at least two children, and one of them is the corroboration.** **AGOSTINO DI GUIDA**, «*vir Gratiae Rivetti, filius Andreae [et] Theresiae Viglioti, aetatis suae annorum **32***», died **24 July 1844** — born about **1812**, five years before his father. And **MADDALENA DI GUIDA**, who married **Angelo Cillo**, son of the late Antonio Cillo and Maria Antonia Romanella, about 1845: «*quondam **Angeli Andreae**, et **Theresiae Viglioti***». **Angelo Andrea named a daughter Maddalena — his own mother's name**, which is exactly what this archive's reconstruction of his parents predicts.
how: A sweep of the Arienzo parish death register for *Guida* — 1,621 distinct pages — run to look for Antonia di Guida's own death. It did not find that. It found her nephew and her niece instead.
why: **A prediction that could have failed is worth more than a match that could not.** Naming a daughter for the paternal grandmother is Campanian practice, not law, so its absence would have proved nothing — but its presence is a check the reconstruction was not built on and did not have to pass. It is recorded as corroboration, not as proof: the proof is still Angelo Andrea's own baptism of 29 November 1791 set against his civil death act of 1817.

what: WHERE ANTONIA DI GUIDA'S DEATH IS NOT — and the page count this entry first gave was eight times too big
was: Her last certain sighting is **27 November 1841**, named without «fu» as the living mother of Giovanni Falco in his death act, and again in Crescenzo Falco's marriage act. After that the archive has nothing.
now: **Not in the Arienzo pages of the parish death register that this sweep reached — and there are far fewer of those than this entry first claimed.** The full-text sweep of collection `M9J1-SMK` (`q.anyPlace=Arienzo`, `q.text=Guida`) returned 2,306 results and 1,621 distinct pages. **Only 229 of those 1,621 pages are Arienzo — fourteen per cent.** The rest are Santa Maria a Vico, San Felice a Cancello, San Prisco, San Marco Evangelista, Lusciano, Carinaro and others. Every page was scanned for *Antonia* within ~200 characters of a Guida-shape **and** a death word — *obiit, mortua, defuncta, uxor, vidua, cadaver, sepulta*. Sixty-seven passages matched and none is her. **The honest statement of this negative is therefore «229 Arienzo pages», not «1,621 pages».**
how: The same loose-shape method that found the di Guida baptisms: sweep on the stable half of the name, then regex the transcripts locally for the unstable half.
why: **This is a bounded negative, and the bound is much tighter than it looked.** 229 pages is nowhere near a complete death register for a parish across 1733–1888, so this rules out very little. It also does **not** exclude that she is entered under her husband's surname — a married woman in these books is often «*uxor Josephi Falco*» with her own surname left off — or that the engine mangled *Guida* past the regex. **A negative whose denominator is wrong is worse than no negative at all**, because it invites everyone afterwards to stop looking.

what: this archive published a 1,621-page negative that was really 229 pages — its own rule, broken the same day it was being quoted
was: An entry added earlier today said Antonia di Guida's death was absent from «**1,621 distinct pages**» of the Arienzo parish death register, and a commit message said the same. Another entry described the di Guida discovery as «**ten acts out of 1,298 pages**».
now: **Both counts were of the result set, not of Arienzo.** Measured per page from `content.recordPlace`: the death sweep is **229 Arienzo pages of 1,621 (14%)**; the baptism sweep that found the di Guida family is **317 of 1,298 (24%)**; a Falco death sweep is **216 of 694 (31%)**; the union of all of them is **406 of 2,256 (18%)**.
how: By doing, belatedly, the thing this archive's own method note has said to do since the day it was written: «*Never state a count as «N pages of X's registers» without checking `content.recordPlace` per entry*».
why: **The 87 per cent figure was measured once, on one collection, and then carried everywhere.** It came from a sample of the MARRIAGE collection `M9J1-9B4`, where it is probably right. It is not a property of the endpoint. On the DEATH collection the same `q.anyPlace=Arienzo` returns **fourteen** per cent, and the rate moves with the query term as well as the collection — *Falco* pulls 31 per cent where *Guida* pulls 14, because *Guida* is common in the neighbouring comuni. **A ratio measured once is not a constant**, and the findings this archive built today are unaffected while the negatives it published are not.

what: the act that makes Gioacchino a son of the founders was machine-read and load-bearing — it is now read from the image, twice filmed
was: The open-questions page said of Gioacchino Falco's baptism of **2 February 1779**: «*The 1779 baptism image — it is transcription only, and it is load-bearing.*» It is the act that makes Gioacchino a documented son of Matteo Falco and Francesca Crisci. **Meanwhile `data/arienzo-parish-acts.tsv` had it marked «image» all along** — a third instance today of this archive disagreeing with itself between a data file and a page.
now: **Read from the image**, on a **second filming** of the same page — `3Q9M-CSD3-13HT-V`, which surfaced beside the known one in a sweep: «*Anno D̄ni Millesimo Septingentesimo Septuagesimo nono **1779**, die vero **secunda 2 Februarii**, R̄dus D̄nus D. **Joseph Migliore** Substitutus baptizavit infantem natum ex **Mattheo Falco, et Francisca Crisci** conjugibus hujus Parochiae, qui nominatus est **Joachim**; Commater fuit **Dorothea d'Addio**, Obstetrix vero **Cecilia Martone**.*» — Antonius Archipr. Romano. Margin «*Joachim Falco*». **Two independent films, two independent machine transcripts and one image reading now agree.**
how: The second film was not searched for. It fell out of a regex run across 2,256 cached transcript pages looking for *Matteo* beside a Falco-shape and a Crisci-shape — the same local-regex pass that was hunting Matteo's marriage.
why: **A second filming is the cheapest corroboration in this archive and nobody had been looking for one.** These parishes were microfilmed more than once, so a load-bearing act read from one photograph can very often be checked against another — different exposure, different focus, and a completely independent pass by the recogniser. **That is now a standing move for any act the line depends on.** It also joined two spellings: the *Dorotea d'Adio* of 1779 and the *Dorothea d'Addio* who is godmother to Maddalena Falco in 1818 are one name, thirty-nine years apart.

what: «QUONDAM» IS NOT A RELIABLE SIGNAL OF DEATH IN THIS PARISH — proved by two acts of the same archpriest, four weeks apart
was: This archive has repeatedly reasoned that **a parent named WITHOUT «quondam» or «fu» was alive** at the date of the act. It is written into at least seven records and two pages, and one open question already half-suspected it — the Angela Falco case of 1829 rested on Pasquale Falco being «named WITHOUT «quondam» … evidence he was then alive».
now: **The signal fails, and here is the pair that proves it, in one register, in one hand, in four weeks.** On **12 July 1802** the archpriest Giacinto Morgillo marries Rosa Falco to Carlo Antonio Morgillo and writes the groom's dead father correctly: «*filium **q.** Caroli Antonii*». On **18 July 1802** **Matteo Falco dies** — his act is on the same film. On **4 August 1802**, seventeen days after that death, the *same* archpriest marries Matteo's son and writes «*non dum uxoratos **Josephum Falco filium Matthæi**, e Franciscæ Crisci*» — **plain «filium», no «q.», for a man buried a fortnight earlier.** Both readings are from the image, at magnification.
how: By reading **Matteo Falco's own death act from the image** — `3Q9M-CSMY-B744-5`, long cited here but marked «image not read» — and then noticing what its date does to a marriage act this archive had already read twice today.
why: **An argument from silence needs the silence to mean something, and here it does not.** The rule is not merely unproven; it is **disproved for the parish Latin register**, by the one scribe whose usage the archive most relies on. The civil acts are a different tradition — an Italian clerk writing «*figlia del fu Crescenzo Rivetti*» is filling a form field, not choosing a word — so the Antenati-based inferences are not directly impeached. **But they are no longer free.** Every «named without «fu», so alive» in this archive is now a *weak* inference that must be carried with the record rather than treated as a fact, and none of them may stand alone against a document.

what: the head of the line, read from the image at last — Matteo Falco's death act
was: Matteo Falco's death — **18 July 1802** — has been the anchor of this whole archive for months, and its citation carried the note «**image not read**, year and day agree in words and digits». The age «annorum 55 circiter», from which his birth about **1747** is derived, was a machine reading.
now: **Read from the image**, margin «*Mattheus Falco*»: «*Anno D̄ni Millesimo octingentesimo secundo **1802**, die vero **decima octava 18 Julii**, **Mattheus Falco vir Franciscæ Crisci**, aetatis suae annorum **55 circiter**, omnibus Sacramentis munitus, in Comm. S. M. E. obiit, et in Archipresbyterali Coemeterio ejus cadaver humatum est.* Hyacinthus Archipr. Morgillo». **The 55 is confirmed**, so b. c.1747 stands. And the act says «**vir**», not «*viduus*» — Francesca Crisci outlived him, as her own act of 31 December 1805 says.
how: It surfaced in a sweep for something else entirely — hunting Matteo's *marriage* through the bride's surname — and the citation's own «image not read» was the prompt to finish it.
why: **The oldest claim in an archive is the least likely to be re-examined**, precisely because everything downstream already depends on it. This one held. The point is that it was checked, four months after it was first published, and that the note admitting it was unread is what made the check happen. **A citation that records its own weakness is doing its job.**

what: WHERE MATTEO FALCO'S MARRIAGE IS NOT — swept through the BRIDE's surname, and this time the denominator is honest
was: An earlier sweep of the parish marriage collection for **Falco** found no marriage of a Matteo Falco in 1,260 pages, and said so with its limits attached — chief among them that **the handwriting engine renders *Falco* as *Falo*, *Falgo*, *Falto*, *Falcone***, so a page where it did so is simply not in the result.
now: **Re-run through FRANCESCA CRISCI instead** — `q.text=Crisci` on collection `M9J1-9B4`. 3,405 results, **1,277 distinct pages, of which 1,173 are Arienzo — ninety-two per cent**, far cleaner than any Falco-led query. Every Arienzo page was regexed locally for a *Matteo*-shape standing near a *Falco*-shape. **The marriage is not there.** What the sweep did return was already held: his death act of 1802, his appearance as a marriage witness in 1759, and — as a control on identity — a *second* **Matteo Falco married to a Crisci**, this one to **Alessandra** Crisci, whose daughter Clementina died in 1892.
how: By taking this archive's own advice — «*a couple marries in the BRIDE's parish, so find Francesca Crisci*» — and applying today's other lesson: query the name the engine renders **most** reliably, then do the loose matching locally where it is free.
why: **This is a better negative than the old one, and it is still not a nil.** It is better because Crisci is dense at Arienzo and so pulls 92 per cent Arienzo where Falco pulls far less, and because the local regex no longer depends on the engine spelling *Falco* correctly. It is still not a nil because **the 1750s and 1760s are thin in these pages** — and thinner than they look, since eighteenth-century years are written in **Latin words**, which no digit-year count sees. **The marriage indexes remain the right instrument**, and the *Joseph* leaf found today shows what they can do: it distinguishes the two Giuseppe Falco of this town by itself.

what: GENERATION SIX'S CHURCH MARRIAGE EXISTS, and the machine had sent it to the wrong family
was: This archive held the **civil** side of Raffaele Falco's marriage to Costanza Maione in 1897 — the processetti dossier, with its birth extract and poverty certificate. **It had no parish act, and no reason to think one had survived.**
now: **The Arienzo parish marriage index has them, at folio 153.** Read from the image off the **R** leaf, `3Q9M-CSMY-B7W5-Q`: «*Raphael Falco et **Constantia MAIONE** — 153*», sitting between «*Raphael Rivetti et M.ᵃ Carmela Loffredo — 152*» and «*Raphael De Masco et Maria Iacone — 154*». **The act exists and the index gives its folio.** It is not yet located: a sweep of 981 Arienzo pages of the marriage collection for *Maione* does not surface the page itself.
how: By detecting index leaves structurally in 2,256 cached transcript pages — many short name-and-number entries, almost no «Anno Domini» — which found **109 index leaves** at Arienzo, **32 of them couple-indexes**, and then reading the one Falco line that mattered.
why: **The machine transcript read the bride as «Constantia MATORE».** Martone is a real and common Arienzo surname, and this archive has an **Anna Martone** on file as Costanza Maione's own mother — so the wrong reading was not merely wrong, it was *plausible*, and it would have attached generation six's marriage to a different woman with a name the archive could corroborate. **The most dangerous OCR error is the one that lands on a name you already hold.** One render at magnification settled it.

what: a third house number on via Camellara — and a Maione living at it
was: The street had two numbers, both from extracts about **Pasquale Falco × Maria Amalia Guida**: **25** at his daughter Pasqualina's birth in 1877 and **5** at his death in 1883 — numbers that do not agree, and which this archive declined to reconcile.
now: **Number 3**, and it is not a Falco house. On **25 November 1880**, «*nella casa posta in via Cumellara **al numero tre***», **Francesco Maione** died at twenty-three, *agricoltore*, «*nato in Arienzo dal fu **Angelo***» — and one of the two men who declared it was **Pasquale Falco himself**, «*di anni quarantadue, giornaliere*», beside Pasquale Carfora, fifty-one. **Forty-two in 1880 and forty-four at his death in 1883: his ages agree across the two acts**, which for these clerks is worth remarking on.
how: It survives as an extract copied into somebody else's marriage dossier and certified at Arienzo on 27 October 1900 — found in a sweep for *Maione* that was looking for something else entirely.
why: **Seventeen years before generation six married Costanza Maione, a Maione household stood on the Falco street**, close enough that a Falco walked to the town hall for them. **No kinship between the two Maione is claimed** — Costanza's father was *Aniello* and this young man's was *Angelo*. But the marriage of 1897 now looks less like two families meeting than like two households on one street. **That is a suggestion, not a finding**, and it is published so that it can be tested rather than quietly assumed.

what: I «corrected» a claim this archive never made — the FindMyPast BMD entry, withdrawn
was: This entry said the archive's verdict «*no electoral roll, no BDM, no cemetery index*» was «measured with a filter on, and wrong», and presented 56 Falco birth, marriage and death records — four of them Queensland — as records «this archive had never seen».
now: **Both halves were false.** The sentence in the method note reads «*Annecchino: still 0. No electoral roll, no BDM, no cemetery index **for any of them**.*» — and *them* is the six passenger records belonging to **this family**, not the surname Falco at large. As written it is correct. And the 56 records were not unseen: the **What has been read** page has carried, since September, «*FindMyPast: all 56 Australian birth, marriage and death records for Falco, and all 31 electoral-roll entries, **read individually***» — together with the conclusion that every Queensland Falco in FindMyPast belongs to **one household in the Burdekin cane country**, «*Giuseppe Falco, born about 1898, who married Mary Rubiolo in 1932*». **That is the finding I announced as mine, four months late.**
how: By reading `site/src/pages/searched.astro` — after publishing the correction, not before.
why: **This is the same mistake twice in one day, and the second time is worse than the first.** The first was a find announced as new. This one is a **correction** announced against a claim that was never made — which is more damaging, because a false correction impugns work that was right. **A correction needs the same check as a find: read what the archive actually says, in the actual file, before contradicting it.** I quoted a memory from summary rather than opening the page it summarised. **What survives of that FindMyPast pass:** 183 identifiers saved to a data file before the trial lapsed, the Home Hill burial place for Giuseppe Falco, and one genuine trap — the id in a result link looks exactly like an NAA barcode and is not.

what: the Maione of Charters Towers — the most attractive wrong answer this archive has been offered
was: Nothing. FindMyPast had never been searched for MAIONE, the surname generation six married into.
now: **It holds a Queensland Maione family, and they are not ours.** **Antonio Maione** appears on the electoral rolls at **Winton in 1913** and **Charters Towers in 1934 and 1939**, division of Kennedy; he died on **28 September 1940**, was buried at **Charters Towers – Lynd**, and was **born in 1864**. Costanza Maione, who married Raffaele Falco at Arienzo in 1897, was born there in **1876** — so an elder brother who had gone out to Queensland would have fitted perfectly, and would have explained why this family later chose **Queensland**. **His death transcript names his father: «Paschariels» — Pasquale. Costanza's father was ANIELLO.** Different household.
how: The lead and its refutation came from the same search, an hour apart: the electoral rolls suggested it, the civil death transcript killed it.
why: **Right surname, right state, right decade, and a motive** — this is exactly the shape of an identification this archive would once have made on «street and trade alone». The father's forename is the only thing that separates them, and it is the thing that was checked. **It is published as a closed lead rather than discarded**, because the next person to search Maione in Queensland will find Antonio first and deserves to know why he was set aside.

what: Filomena Annecchino's birth at Forchia in 1897 — the ANSWER WAS ALREADY IN THIS ARCHIVE, and the open question was stale
was: Her birth act has never been found. Antenati holds **no Forchia births for 1897** in any fondo; FamilySearch's Benevento collection **does** cover Forchia in 1897 — a control on the surname IULIANO returns about thirty records in every year 1894–1899 — and **all eight of her siblings are indexed while she is not**. The open-questions page had therefore put a second possibility in writing: «*and this archive has not been willing to say it before — **SHE WAS NOT BORN AT FORCHIA IN 1897**. The date and the place come from the family tree, and the tree has been wrong before.*»
now: **The question was already answered, and not by the grave.** `data/qld-bdm.tsv` has held her Queensland death registration — **1988/6856**, died 10 August 1988, born **1897**, **father CARMINE ANECHINO** — marked «ours», for longer than this session. The open-questions page went on saying «*she was not born at Forchia in 1897*» while the file that contradicts it sat in the same repository. **Find a Grave added a second witness and a birthplace in words — «1897, Forchia, Provincia di Caserta» — and nothing else.** The archive's own figure is better than the memorial's: **10 April 1897**.
how: Not by searching a cemetery. By finally reading `data/qld-bdm.tsv` — after publishing a claim that a cemetery had settled it.
why: **The substance stands and the credit does not.** Filomena WAS born at Forchia in 1897; the act is missing, not the birth; and the doubt on /open-questions should have been withdrawn long ago. **But it was withdrawable from evidence already in this repository**, and saying that a gravestone settled it was wrong. **A fifth stale page, found the same day as the other four** — and this one was stale against a file rather than against another page, which is harder to see and therefore worse.

what: «A GENERATION THIS ARCHIVE DID NOT HAVE» — WITHDRAWN THE SAME DAY. It had it, in four files.
was: The line ran: Raffaele Falco × Costanza Maione (1897) → **Carminantonio Falco × Filomena Annecchino** → Carmine, who reached Brisbane in 1964. Between Carminantonio and the living generation the archive had an infant son, **Aniello**, dead at nine months at Forchia in 1937, and little else.
now:
**This entry was wrong, and wrong in the way this archive most often is.** Everything it announced was already held:

- `data/nudgee-burials.tsv` holds **all five Nudgee graves**, with the same plots — CHAP-082-B1 and B2, V-0946, V-0947, V-0949 — and the same dates.
- `data/qld-bdm.tsv` holds **all three Queensland death registrations with the parents already transcribed**: 1985/3063, 1988/6856 and 1988/8547, each marked «ours».
- `data/naa-records.tsv` holds the Brisbane naturalisation file **J25 1972/4964 — «Falco, Raffaele [Italian, born 1925]; wife Caterina [nee Zampiello]; and children Filomena and Antonio»**. The marriage this entry called a discovery is on the cover of a government file.
- And the claim that it is **«not established whether Caterina descends from Angelo Zampiello of Arpaia» was false**: the family tree this archive harvests lists her among his five daughters — Francesca, Tommasina, **Caterina**, Rosina and Raffaela.

**The archive also held better figures than the ones offered here**: Carminantonio born **11 January 1901**, not «1900»; Filomena born **10 April 1897**, not «1897».
how: By reading this archive's own method memory two hours too late. It says in one line: «*five Nudgee burials that corrected two death dates in the tree*» and «*two Falco brothers married two Zampiello sisters*».
why: **I spent this session documenting that an archive of ten thousand pages contradicts itself, and then did the thing itself — in the opposite direction.** Four times today a stale page was caught still asking a question the data had answered. This is the mirror image: **a find announced as new because the finder did not check what was already held.** The rule that catches both is the same one, and it is the rule I was quoting: **check against existing holdings in the same pass — before publishing, not after.** **What actually survives from the Find a Grave pass** is small and worth keeping: five memorial ids giving a second independent witness to burials known from the cemetery's own register, the fact that Caterina is the only Zampiello grave in Australia on that site, and a genuine trap — its location ids are not guessable, and a guessed one returns Switzerland while reporting «Australia».

what: the Zampiello had no household in this archive at all — and a civil act documenting them was sitting unused
was: `data/households.tsv` is where this archive keeps its reconstructed family groups, with a source against every person. **It contained not one Zampiello row.** The family's other main line — the one generation eight married into, twice — existed here only as tree entries and as 260 rows of a name index. **Angelo Zampiello and Giuseppa Ferrara were carried on the authority of a family tree.**
now: **They are documented, and the document was already harvested.** The marriage act of **26 August 1939 at Arpaia** — `an_ud1197203`, in `data/antenati-zampiello-annecchino.tsv` and `data/antenati-names-zampiello-arpaia.tsv` — records **Tommasina Zampiello**, born Arpaia 1921, «*Coniuge = **Michele Ruggiero**; Padre = **Angelo Zampiello**; Madre = **Giuseppa Ferraro***». The household now stands in `households.tsv` with **every person graded**: Angelo and Giuseppa and Tommasina from the act; Caterina and Francesca from the cemetery register and NAA file **J25 1972/4964**; Raffaela from the tree alone; and **Rosina named and nothing more, because she is living**.
how: By reading the archive's own Antenati name index for the 1920s instead of searching anything new. **The 1920s hold exactly one row in that file, and it is this act.**
why: **Harvesting is not holding.** 260 rows were pulled from the Arpaia name index and the one row that documents the family's own parents was never promoted into a household. That is the same failure as a stale page, one level down: **the fact was in the repository and nothing pointed at it.** **And a spelling, left visible rather than resolved:** the act writes **FERRARO**, the tree writes **FERRARA**. Campanian clerks move between the two freely and this archive does not choose. **What is still missing** is Angelo Zampiello's own birth act — Arpaia 1895 is one of the two volumes Antenati never digitised, its shelf-marks running consecutively and skipping the year — and the birth acts of **Caterina (1925)** and **Francesca (1928)**, which are not in the indexed range either.

what: the Annecchino had no household either — and the sibling spacing quietly supports Filomena's missing 1897
was: **`households.tsv` held not one Annecchino row**, though `data/annecchino-benevento-fs.tsv` has carried 370 harvested births for months and the open-questions page has listed Filomena's siblings in prose. Generation seven's wife's own parents were nowhere in the archive's household file.
now: **Two Forchia households, both from the civil births.** **CARMINE ANNECCHINO × MARIA CARFORA** with nine children — Giacinta 1883, Agata 1884, Giacomo 1887, a second Agata 1889, the **twins Lucia and Alfonso both registered 2 August 1892**, Alfonso Carmine 1894, **Filomena 1897 (no act)** and Giacomo 1901. The repeated names mark the children who died: a second Agata after 1884, a second Alfonso after the twin, a second Giacomo after 1887. And separately **SABATINO ANNECCHINO × MARIANTONIA CARFORA**, six children 1861–1870 — **a second Annecchino man married to a second Carfora woman**, recorded and not interpreted.
how: By grouping a file this archive harvested and never promoted — the same failure as the Zampiello, found in the same hour.
why: **The spacing is the find.** Filomena's siblings arrive in 1883, 1884, 1887, 1889, 1892, 1892, 1894 — and then nothing until **1901**. A household producing a child every two or three years does not simply stop for seven and start again. **A birth in 1897 fills the gap exactly.** That is a third independent line of support for a date whose act has never been found, after the Queensland death registration and the grave — **and it is support, not proof**, which is why it is written here rather than on the direct line. **And a name deliberately NOT joined:** Sabatino's son **Carmine Maria Annecchino, born 13 February 1867 at Forchia**, is the right name in the right town and would make a tidy grandfather. **He would have been sixteen when Giacinta was born.** The archive does not attach him.

what: generation five had no household — the last of the four lines that were missing one
was: **`households.tsv` held not one Arricale row**, and no household for **Carmine Antonio Falco × Giovanna Arricale** — generation five, the parents of the Raffaele who married Costanza Maione in 1897. Their children existed only as tree entries and as a paragraph in a note about a marriage dossier.
now: **The household stands, with every child graded.** **RAFFAELE** (b. 6 Apr 1873) is documented by the birth extract in his own 1897 dossier. **ANGELA ROSA** is documented by her banns of August 1902: «*FALCO ANGELA ROSA, di anni **ventidue**, contadina, figlia di **CARMINANTONIO** … e figlia di **ARRICALE GIOVANNA***», marrying **Francesco Esposito** of San Felice a Cancello. **MARIA GIUSEPPA** (1875), **a first ANGELA ROSA** (b. 31 Jan 1878, d. 6 Feb 1879) and **GIUSEPPE** (1883) are tree only, and are marked so.
how: By grouping the tree file by parent-couple and then setting each child against the documents already written up in `notes/processetto-falco-maione-1897.md` — the fourth line in one afternoon that had its evidence harvested and never promoted.
