Until that is reconciled, every note generated about generation four's parentage will say the archive identifies generation three as «someone else». **That is a wrong sentence on a live page and it is not mine to quietly rewrite.**

what: The contested parents now carry their verdict on the record, not only in prose
was: The chart at `/bloodline` could say only **that** eight people's parents disagree, and how many kinds of source were involved. It could not say **which** claim this archive stands behind, because the reasoning lived in prose and the edges themselves carried nothing.
now:
**Every contested edge carries a verdict and a reason**, written in `site/src/data/parent-verdicts.json` and applied by the person-graph builder. Three kinds: **retired** for a claim disproved or superseded, **same-as** for a second record of someone already listed and deliberately unmerged, and silence for an accepted parent. **All eight people are now down to two accepted parents or fewer.**

**Two claims were disproved outright today, both on Vincenzo Morgillo.** **GAETANA LAUDATO** was «*di anni settantotto*» at her death in March 1816, so born about **1738**, and she stands in that house as **Simone Morgillo's widow** — a generation above its head. Vincenzo was twenty-nine in May 1828, born about **1799**. She was sixty-one at his birth and is not his mother. **GIUSEPPE MORGILLO** is the father of a **different Vincenzo Morgillo — an infant of FOUR DAYS who died on 25 January 1816 in strada Salvatorella**. This one lived in strada Cappuccini and declared two deaths at the Capuchin monastery in the 1820s. Merged on the forename alone.
how: Following the reading offered on the chart: that the repeated third parent across four Cossi siblings, and the same shape on Vincenzo Morgillo, looked like **one systematic error rather than several** — and the suggestion to check whether the extra parent was a godparent, a witness or a second marriage misread. For the Morgillo it was none of those: **it was a dead infant of the same name.**
why:
**The archive was already right about most of this and simply could not say so.** The Cossi third parent is a correction it published itself; the doubled Andreana is a merge it refuses on principle; the Falcone pair is an ancestor it examined and dropped. Only Vincenzo Morgillo held real errors, and both were the same kind — **a name doing the work that a date and a street should do.** 

**The merges are still not made.** «Andrea / Andreana Crisci» and «Andreana Crisci» are marked as one woman under two spellings and left as two records, because there are **two Andreana Crisci in the tree** and no date yet separates them. That is a judgement for whoever next reads the register, and the record now says so in those words instead of leaving the chart to guess.

what: Alfonso Diglio's second wife was ANNA MARIA CRISCI, not Cossi — found by auditing my own week
was: Published here yesterday, from the 1827 marriage tavola: Alfonso Diglio «*married again on 2 April 1827 to **ANNA MARIA COSSI**, daughter of Salvatore Cossi*». That remarriage is what dated the death of his first wife, Maria Falco, and so it is load-bearing.
now: **CRISCI.** At eight times magnification the word is **C–r–i–sc–i**: a narrow **r** after the C and a **dotted i**, with no round «o». Set beside the 1818 entry for Arcangelo **Cossi**, magnified the same way, the difference is plain — that one is C–**o**–ss–i, a round letter with no dot.
how: Not by rechecking this entry, but by **auditing every surname I read in this hand over the past two days** after re-breaking the Cioffi correction earlier today. Three readings were in the ambiguous class. One was already wrong and fixed this morning, one was confirmed right, and this is the third.
why:
**The audit was worth running and I should have run it unprompted.** Three readings, two errors, and the third only confirmed because it was tested rather than assumed. 

**The date does not move.** Alfonso Diglio still remarried on 2 April 1827, which still puts Maria Falco's death before it, and her death act of 25 April 1826 still names her parents outright. What changes is the bride's family, and with it any future attempt to trace her. 

The deeper point is that this parish hand carries **three surnames that collapse into one shape** — COSSI, CRISCI and CIOFFI — and this archive has now been caught by all three in a single week. The test that separates them is not judgement, it is magnification: **the dot after the C, the round o, the r.** That is now the standing rule for this hand.

what: Two days of findings reach the site — the household files are one file again
was:
This archive kept its reconstructed families in **two files that had drifted apart**: `data/households.tsv`, which its own README and research notes call the family file, and `site/src/data/households.json`, **which is what the site is actually built from**. Nothing synced them. The TSV held **66 households**, the JSON **53**, and they differed in both directions — **12 households existed only in the JSON, 25 only in the TSV**. 

So **Sara Falco, Giuseppe Nunzio Falco, Clementina Diglio, Giuseppa Cioffi, the Angelandrea join, Maria Falco's identification, five children for Angela Falco and generation three's own wedding day were described in the corrections log and were not in the archive's data at all.**
now:
**Merged, additively — nothing in either file was deleted.** `households.json` goes from 53 households and 209 members to **77 and 337**. The person graph goes from **549 people to 626**, and the site from **10,147 pages to 10,284**. 

**And `npm run check` now refuses a release whose TSV is ahead of the JSON**, naming the rows that would not reach the site.
how: A dry run first, printing exactly what would be added and confirming nothing would be removed; then the merge; then the gates. The merge itself **introduced three duplicates** — one Chiara Rivetti under two spellings, two Pasquale Falco rows that had already been split apart earlier today — because the de-duplication keyed on the exact person string. Found by comparing every added name against the existing names in the same household, and repaired.
why:
**This is the failure that produced all the others this week.** A retracted reading survived in the TSV as a live household name, and I read it, trusted it and **republished a correction the archive had already made** — the Cioffi household, twice in one day. 

The general shape is worth naming: **an archive that keeps its working file and its published file apart will, given time, publish from whichever one is stale.** The corrections log said the right thing the whole time; the data said nothing at all. 

The guard is the durable part. A note describing this problem would have been read by nobody; a check that fails the build will be read by whoever next writes a row.

what: Generation three exists again — one bracket was hiding it
was: **No person in this archive carried generation three.** The line file names it — **VINCENZO FALCO** — and the person graph never bound the two, so the direct line ran 1, 2, **—**, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. The consequence was live on the site: every note generated about generation four's parentage read «*This archive does not [make Vincenzo Falco a parent of generation 4]: it identifies generation 3 as **someone else***» — **a sentence that was not true, about the man the whole line descends through.**
now:
**All nine generations are assigned.** The matcher requires the ancestor's name AND the spouse's to agree. `line.json` spells her «*Adriana **(Andreana)** Crisci*»; every act spells her **ANDREANA CRISCI**; and the archive's own name-cleaning routine **strips brackets before the comparison**, so the file's only surviving form was «Adriana Crisci» and the two never met. 

The name-variant helper now reads the **unclean** name and emits the bracketed alternative as well — the same thing it already did for slashes, «*Andrea / Andreana Crisci*». **No «someone else» note survives, and no one in the archive has more than two accepted parents.**
how: By instrumenting the matcher rather than reasoning about it. The first fix was written in the right place and did nothing, because the function's second line had already thrown the brackets away — the test only found that out when the debug line printed `gen_of= None` beside a name that matched.
why:
**A punctuation mark between two spellings of one woman's forename cost this archive a generation of its own direct line**, and the visible symptom was a page confidently denying a parentage it asserts everywhere else. 

The fix is small and the lesson is not: this file cleans names to keep old URLs alive, and that same cleaning silently governs whether two records can ever be recognised as one. **Anything that normalises a name for one purpose will be used for another.** 

Two smaller things fell out of the same pass. **Three «people» who were couples** — rows where a marriage was recorded against «Vincenzo Falco & Andreana Crisci» as though that were a person — are re-attributed to the husband. And the builder's refusal to merge **Pasquale Rivetti** with his own grandfather of the same name is left standing: that refusal is the protection, and both men keep their own record.

what: The two Andreana Crisci are separated — and the deacon gets his own death back
was: The family tree holds **two women called Andreana Crisci**, and the person graph refused to merge either with the registers' Andreana, because **this archive does not merge two records on a matching name**. Her page was drawn twice, and both Antonio and Raffaele Falco listed her twice over.
now:
**Separated by husband, and the right one merged.** Tree `4512467` — «*Andrea / Andreana Crisci (Falco)*» — is married to **VINCENZO FALCO**, and its own note carries her baptism: «*baptised ADRIANA, 30 November 1796, daughter of **Arcangelo Crisci and Sara Ruggiero***». That is the reading the **1814 marriage index** gave independently yesterday. Tree `4512381` is married to a different man, **Gioacchino / Guglielmo Falco**, and stays a separate woman. 

The merge was not forced: it fell out of fixing generation three. The builder already held a rule for exactly this — «*the couple chooses*» — and it had never been able to run, because it depends on the same bracket-blind name comparison. **Merges refused fall from eight to five; merged-from-both rises from ten to twenty-nine.**
how: Reading the two tree records side by side and separating them on the husband, then rebuilding — at which point the archive's own dormant rule did the work.
why:
**Three more duplicates fell out of the same pass, and one of them was hiding a man's death.** 

**LUIGI FALCO** was two records in one household — a baptism of December 1819 under «Luigi (Aloysius) Falco» and a death of 16 December 1864 under «Luigi Falco». One man, forty-five years, two people. 

Worse: **the burial of 27 November 1841 was sitting on DON GIOVANNI THE DEACON'S record.** The old machine-transcript row was still filed under the plain name, so the elder brother's death and the deacon's birth of 6 April 1825 were on one page — the exact conflation this archive spent yesterday proving false. Re-attributed. 

And the deacon's **own** death act — read from the image on 13 September, «*DON GIOVANNI FALCO … di professione DIACONO*», 26 November 1849 — **was in the corrections log and in no data file at all.** It is in the household now. Its declarants are **Gennaro and Francesco Cioffi** of strada Camellara, which is the same family whose surname this archive mis-read twice this week.

what: The elder Giovanni Falco is not in the birth registers of 1816 or 1817
was: His burial was read from the image yesterday: «*JOANNES FALCO filius Josephi et Antoniae di Guida, aetate sua **annorum 24 circiter***», **27 November 1841**. That puts his birth between November 1816 and November 1817 if the age is anywhere near right, and he is the brother whose existence forced this archive to accept **two living sons named Giovanni** in one house.
now:
**Both years are read out, act by act, and he is in neither.** 

**1817** (`an_ua14414`, 109 acts, images 4–46): **not one Falco in the entire year.** 
**1816** (`an_ua14413`, 62 acts, images 4–64): **one Falco act only** — Domenico Falco, born 25 November to **Giuseppe Falco, 36, massaro di campo of STRADA COSTA**, and Gelsomina Vigliotta. That is the OTHER Giuseppe Falco, already held, and no Giovanni.
how: The declarant band swept across every opening of both volumes — this form puts a whole act on one half-page, so both halves carry a separate «*è comparso …*».
why:
**A negative worth the reading, because it narrows a question this archive opened yesterday.** Three things remain possible and the archive prefers none: the stated age is wrong, which this register does constantly; he was born in a year not yet read — 1815, or 1818 to 1820; or his birth is **only in the parish register** and never reached the comune. 

**The 1817 result is the stranger one.** Giuseppe Falco and Antonia di Guida were an active household — a daughter Maddalena on 7 June 1818, sons through the 1820s — and **the whole of 1817 holds no Falco birth at all**, from any of the four Falco houses this archive tracks at Arienzo. A year that empty is itself a fact about the volume, not only about the family. 

**Citation slip corrected in passing:** this archive cites Domenico Falco's act as `img59l`. It is on **image 60**, left page.

what: The printed year on a Bourbon form is not the year of the act
was: Volumes in this series have been identified by **ark arithmetic** and by the catalogue label, and — when those were doubted — by reading the year off the act itself.
now:
**Reading the year off the act is not enough either.** These registers were printed in batches with a year already set in type. When the stock outlasted the year, **the clerk struck the printed word and wrote the true year above it by hand**: «*L'Anno mille ottocento ~~sedici~~ **diciassette** a' dì sedici del mese di Febrajo*». 

So `an_ua14414` reads **sedici** in print on every page and **is the register of 1817**. Likewise `an_ua14415` is printed *sedici* and is **1818**.
how: Caught because the printed year disagreed with the volume's catalogue label, and the manuscript correction is small, set above the line, and easy to read straight past — which is exactly what happened here first: the volume was called 1816 on the strength of the print, and the arithmetic was accused of slipping when it had not.
why:
**Three different ways of naming a volume have now each been wrong in this series within one week** — the ark arithmetic after 1835, the catalogue label, and now the printed year. The only reliable identification is **the manuscript**: the correction above the printed word, the dates in the entries, and the closing certificate. 

And the cost of getting it wrong is not a mislabelled file. It is a **false negative**: a year declared empty of Falco on the strength of a volume that was a different year.

what: Giuseppe Nunzio Falco does not die at Arienzo between 1824 and 1830
was: Published this week as **a new son for generation three** — «*GIUSEPPE NUNZIO FALCO, born 25 March 1824 at half past twenty-three hours*», to Vincenzo Falco and Andreana Crisci of strada Camellara — and published **as a birth and nothing more**, because nothing else was known of him. No marriage names him; the 1825 death register, read act by act, does not hold him.
now:
**Seven consecutive annual death indexes read, and he is in none of them: 1824, 1825, 1826, 1827, 1828, 1829, 1830.** That is the whole of his early childhood. 

What those seven years DO hold for this surname is already published here: **Maddalena** and **Clemente Falco** in 1825, and **Maria Falco**, wife of Alfonso Diglio, in 1826. Nothing else — 1824, 1827, 1828 and 1829 have **no F section at all**, the index running Diglio straight to Fattoruso, or Esposito straight to Giglio.
how: The «Morti, indice» series, `an_ua14271` + (year − 1809) — one to seven images a year, each line giving the dead person, their town, their trade, **both parents** and the date. The same series slips as the marriage indexes do: **1836 is missing**, and from `an_ua14298` the labels run a year ahead.
why:
**A child who is born and never dies in his own parish is the ordinary shape of a man who lived.** This archive has been treating Giuseppe Nunzio as probably dead in infancy because nothing followed his birth act; seven years of indexes say the opposite, and the burden now sits on finding him alive rather than explaining his absence. 

**It also raises a name.** Vincenzo Falco and Andreana Crisci have a daughter **NUNZIATA** who married in November 1855 and is known from that act alone. A son christened **Giuseppe Nunzio** and a daughter called Nunziata in one household is either a coincidence or a family name being carried — and this archive has watched that family reuse names relentlessly. **It is not claimed; it is the next thing to test, in the marriage indexes after 1849 and in the death registers from 1831.** 

One check the sweep made and did not need: **ROSA FALCO, daughter of Matteo Falco and Francesca Crisci, dead 16 October 1830** as the wife of Carlantonio Morgillo — a daughter of the founders, and **already held here since before this week**.

what: WITHDRAWN as a discovery — the printed-year trap was already written down, and so was the 1817 nil
was: Published here **today**, as a method finding: «*The printed year on a Bourbon form is not the year of the act… `an_ua14414` reads «sedici» in print on every page and IS the register of 1817*». And, as a bounded negative: «*1817, 109 acts: **not one Falco in the entire year***».
now:
**Both were already in this archive.** `notes/1817-birth-register-progress.md`, written before today, says: «*Result: no Falco at all. **Not one Falco appears in the 1817 births** — not as a father, not as a declarant*», and, in its second line, «*As in 1818, every act is pre-printed **«sedici»** and corrected by hand to **«diciassette»***». 

`notes/1816-birth-register-progress.md` likewise records **1816 read in full, acts 1–123**, and carries the archival label «*THIS INDEX HAS BEEN MICROFILMED ALREADY*» — which was reported here yesterday as a discovery about the 1825 tavola.
how: Found only because David asked whether outstanding findings were being tracked centrally. They are — in `notes/`, 83 progress files, one per register year, and in `notes/QUEUE.md`, a 640-line research queue **last updated on 13 September and never opened during two days of work.**
why:
**The reading was duplicated and the conclusion was re-derived.** The negative stands — 1816 and 1817 really do hold no Giovanni — but it was already this archive's negative, and the hours spent re-establishing it bought nothing. 

**This is the fourth instance in one week of the same failure**, and the pattern is now unmistakable: the Nudgee graves were in three files when they were announced; the Cioffi correction was standing in the household file when it was re-broken; the deacon's death act was in the corrections log and in no data file; and now a completed sweep and its method note were in `notes/` while both were done again. 

**Every one of them would have been caught by reading the archive's own index before starting.** The failure is not carelessness inside a task — the work has been careful. It is **starting a task without asking what is already known**, which is a thing that happens before the care begins.

what: Two more children, from thirteen years of death indexes read by their surname column alone
was: The Arienzo death indexes for **1831–1843** were the one stretch between the years this archive had read act by act. Thirteen annual volumes, fifty-five images.
now:
**Two children this archive did not have.** 

**PASQUALE FALCO, 30 October 1838** — «*71. Falco Pasquale | **Falco Francesco, e Falco Raffaela***». That is the **first-cousin marriage**: Francescantonio Falco, son of Pasquale and Chiara Rivetti, and Raffaela Falco, daughter of Giuseppe and Antonia di Guida, married 16 July 1832. Their children now run **Carmina 1832, Pasqualina 1836, Pasquale 1838, Clemente 1853** — four, three of them dead small. 

**MATTEO FALCO, 24 August 1842** — «*55. Falco Matteo | **Falco Michele, e Vigliotta Antonia***», a third child for **Michelangelo Falco and Mariantonia Vigliotta**, and the first of that house not called Anna.
how: Not by reading fifty-five pages. **The question a death index is asked is «is there a Falco on this page», and that question lives in one column** — so the surname column was cropped out of every page and tiled eight to a sheet. Four sheets instead of fifty-five reads. Every candidate was then magnified to the word before it was accepted, and **one was rejected that way**: a row that looked like FALCO on the tile is CRISCI at magnification.
why:
**The years break into three kinds and the difference matters.** *Already held*: 1831, 1832, 1833 — Anna, Giovanna, Carmina, Pasquale, every one of them already in this archive, and each checked before it was claimed. *Empty*: 1835, 1837, 1839, 1840, 1843 — five years with no Falco at all. *New*: 1838 and 1842. 

**And one year is not a negative and must not be read as one.** The **1834 index is a single leaf covering A to C and marked END** — this archive recorded that caution weeks ago and it holds. Any Falco who died in 1834 is invisible here, and only the register itself will show them. 

The Michele/Michelangelo reading is published **with its doubt attached**: the forenames are shortened, which this register does constantly, and the surname VIGLIOTTA is the half that identifies. A separate Michele Falco married to an Antonia is not impossible, and only the act would settle it.

what: Six children, all of them buried small — and a conflict this archive will not resolve by choosing
was: Three rows were seen in the death indexes yesterday and **deliberately not published**, because the crop missed the line twice and this archive had already mis-read that hand three times in a week. They went onto the work list as an item instead of into the archive as findings.
now:
**All three verified at magnification. Two are real children.** 

**GIUSEPPE CIOFFI, 5 December 1830** — a *second* Giuseppe, the first having died on 25 March 1824 aged five. **MARIANTONIA CIOFFI, 3 December 1832** — a *second* Mariantonia, the first dead on 23 October 1828. 

So **Francesco Cioffi and Maria Falco buried six children in nine years**: Antonia 1823, Giuseppe 1824, Giuseppa 1825, Mariantonia 1828, Giuseppe again 1830, Mariantonia again 1832. **Not one of them is known to have reached adulthood**, and both of the repeated names were given again after the first child carrying them had died.
how: The month on the 1832 act is not written out — it reads «*A 3 detto*». It is fixed by **the ditto chain**: act 62 on the same page says «*A 2 Xbre 1832*», act 63 says «*A detto dì*», act 64 says «*A 3 detto*». Three rows of a clerk's shorthand, read in order.
why:
**The third row is the one worth keeping open.** The index reads «*14. **Morgillo RAFFAELA** … A 9 **MARZO** 1832*». This archive already holds, from the act itself, «*RAFFAELE Morgillo, **22**, **contadino***», died **9 May 1832**. Same day of the month, different month, different ending, different sex. 

Either Carlantonio Morgillo and Rosa Falco lost two children nine weeks apart, or **one death has been read two ways** — *Marzo* and *Maggio* begin alike, and so do *Raffaela* and *Raffaele*. The act is the stronger source for an age and a trade; the index is a copy. **This archive is not going to pick.** Reading atto 14 of 1832 against the act already held settles it in one pass, and until then both readings stand on the record. 

Rosa Falco is the founders' daughter, so whichever it is, it is Matteo Falco's grandchild.

what: 1859 opened — three Falco deaths, a household this archive has never seen, and no Giuseppe
was: The Arienzo death registers were read out for **1844–1858** and stopped there. **Giuseppe Falco was alive and named as a living father in April 1854**, at about seventy-four, and his death has never been found. The «Morti, indice» series ends at 1847, so everything after it needed the registers themselves.
now:
**1859 carries its own alphabetical tavola, bound in at the front**, giving both parents and the date — and it holds **three Falco deaths, none of them known here**. 

**MARIA FALCO**, 4 March, and **RAFFAELE FALCO**, 17 August, both «*di MICHELE, ed AMBROGIO MARIA GIOVANNA*» — **a Falco household this archive has never recorded.** No Ambrogio has ever appeared here as a Falco wife. 

**CARMELA FALCO**, 4 August, «*di MICHELE, e VIGLIATO ANT[ONI]A*» — a **fourth child** for Michelangelo Falco and Mariantonia Vigliotta, alongside two Anna and the Matteo found earlier today. 

**No Giuseppe Falco and no Vincenzo Falco in the year.**
how: The index is not where the earlier volumes keep it. It is **bound at the front**, and it **runs across both pages of each opening** — the first sweep read only the right-hand pages and came away with the sections jumping C to G, which would have made Diglio, the commonest surname in this town, vanish from a whole year. **A missing letter is the tell that half the table is on the other page.**
why:
**Three deaths and not one of them answers the question the volume was opened for**, which is worth saying plainly: Giuseppe Falco is still alive as far as this archive can show, and 1860 to 1865 remain. 

**1860 has no index at all** — front or back — and ends at act 103. That year is an act-by-act read, and the work list now says so rather than leaving it to be rediscovered. 

The Michele/Michelangelo caution is repeated deliberately. This index clips both forenames, and it wrote the surname **VIGLIATO** where every other source writes **VIGLIOTTA**. That is the half that identifies, and the act is what would settle it.

superseded.what: Arienzo deaths 1859 read from the year's own index — and the series stops at 1865
superseded.note: **Published the day before, from the same tavola.** The three acts, the index bound at the front and the absence of Vincenzo were all set out on 14 September, including the household this entry calls one «*this archive has never recorded*» — which was recorded there by name, with what it had previously been known by. **This is a duplicate, not a discovery.**

what: Sara Falco lived, and married — the child found three days ago now has a husband
was: **SARA FALCO** was found on 14 September in the 1828 alphabetical tavola, four minutes before this archive published a false negative saying the year held no Falco. She was known as **a birth and nothing else**: 19 December 1828, strada Camellara, declared by a midwife. Nothing said whether she reached adulthood.
now:
**She married at twenty-six.** «*Atto di solenne promessa di matrimonio, **Num. d'ordine 6**, 14 FEBBRAJO 1855*»: «*…sono comparsi **ANTONIO MAURO** maggiore, nato in Arienzo, di professione **FRUTTAJOLO**, domiciliato **strada Croce**, figlio di **Domenico** … e di **Vincenza Grosso** … e **SARA FALCO** maggiore, nata in Arienzo, domiciliata **STRADA CAMELLARA**, figlia di **VINCENZO** di professione **COLONO** … e di **ANDREANA**…*» 

The **INDICAZIONE** margin carries the other half: the parroco returned the certificate for the church celebration on the **fifteenth of February**. Promise on the Wednesday, wedding on the Thursday.
how: By answering a different question. The work list asked **what finding aid covers Arienzo marriages after 1849**, because the «Matrimoni, indice» series stops there and Nunziata Falco married in 1855. The answer is that **the register itself is the finding aid**: `an_ua14213` + (year − 1809), twenty-eight to thirty-seven acts a year, and every act names **both spouses, both sets of parents, and the parish celebration date in the margin**. Sara fell out of the first volume opened.
why:
**A trade this archive has never met.** Nine generations of *bracciali*, *contadini*, *coloni* and *massari*, one deacon — and Sara married a **FRUTTAJOLO**, a fruitseller, off strada Croce. No Mauro has stood in these households before. 

**And a negative in the same volume.** **NUNZIATA FALCO**, her sister, is held here as marrying on «*13 [Nov] 1855*» — the month in brackets, this archive's own mark for a reading it does not trust. **She is not in the 1855 promise register**, whose twenty-eight acts were read line by line. Two daughters of one house marry in one year and the civil register has only one of them. Either the parish date is wrong, or Nunziata married at her husband's comune — which would invert the rule this archive has proved twice, that a couple marries in the **bride's** parish.

what: Sara Ruggiero stood godmother to six Falco households — and this archive learned her name yesterday
was: **SARA RUGGIERO** entered this archive **yesterday**, from one line of the 1814 marriage index: «*Andreana Crisci … **Arcangelo, e SARA RUGGIERO***». Before that she was «*[Rosae] Ruggiero*» — a bracketed guess from a machine transcript of the parish act. She had no other record of any kind.
now:
**«Matrina fuit SARA RUGGIERO» appears on TEN PAGES of the parish baptism harvest.** She stood godmother to children of at least **six Falco households**: 

**Pasquale Falco & Chiara Rivetti** — generation four. **Giuseppe Falco & Gelsomina Vigliotta** of strada Costa. **Gioacchino Falco & Vittoria Cimmino** — the founder's son. **Domenico Crisci & Margarita Falco**, on three separate pages. **Antonio Morgillo & Rosa Falco** — the founder's daughter. And **Vincenzo Falco & Andreana Crisci**, which is **her own daughter's house**. A Giuseppe Falco and Antonia di Guida baptism carries her as well.
how: Looking for something else. The work list asked for **Sara Falco's parish baptism**, and the lead was a cached index leaf reading «*Sara Falco fol. 47*». Searching the harvest for «Sara» beside a Falco returned nine segments, and **eight of them were not Sara Falco at all** — they were Sara Ruggiero, signing as godmother, over and over.
why:
**One woman is standing at the font for both of Matteo Falco's sons, for two of his daughters' families, for the other Giuseppe Falco of strada Costa, and for her own daughter.** That is not a neighbour. This archive has spent weeks proving that at Arienzo the surname identifies nobody and the street, the trade and the godparent do — and here is a godparent doing exactly that work, across six houses the archive has been carefully keeping apart. 

It also settles a caution raised on 14 September. When **Sara Falco** was born on 19 December 1828, the midwife who declared her was **GELSOMINA RUGGIERO**, and this archive wrote that no kinship was claimed because the name was common. With Andreana's mother now firmly a **Ruggiero** and a Ruggiero standing godmother in six Falco households, **the Ruggiero are plainly inside this family's circle** — and that is still not a claim that Gelsomina and Sara were sisters. It is a reason to go and find out. 

**Everything here is at transcript strength.** Ten machine readings, none read from the image, and the OCR is visibly bad — «Andreana Cini», «Tesummina Vigliotta», «Cara Ricesta». Published as a pattern, not as ten facts.

what: Two Arcangelo Crisci — Andreana's father is not Anna Falco's husband
was: The name **ARCANGELO CRISCI** stood in this archive twice and nothing separated the two. Once as **Andreana Crisci's father**, from the 1814 marriage index read yesterday — «*Arcangelo, e Sara Ruggiero*». Once as **Anna Falco's husband**, from her death act of 23 August 1820 — «*moglie di Arcangelo Crisci*». If they were one man, this line's own great-great-grandmother married into the house her father had married into, and nobody had checked.
now:
**Two men, and the 1817 birth register holds them both.** 

«*è comparso **ARCANGELO CRISCI** di anni **CINQUANTADUE**, contadino, domiciliato … **strada CAMELLARA** … e da **SARA RUGGIERO** sua moglie legittima d'anni **quarantacinque***» — b. c.**1765**, and Andreana's father. 

«*è comparso **ARCANGELO CRISCI** di anni **TRENTA**, contadino … **strada CAPODICONCA** … e da **MARIA MARTONE***» — b. c.**1787**. 

**Twenty-two years apart, two streets, two wives, both declaring a birth in the same volume.** Andreana's father is not Anna Falco's husband.
how: Not from an image at first. `data/sweep-people.tsv` — this archive's own harvest — **already carried both ages**, «*aged 52*» and «*aged 30*», both 1817, both contadini. It has carried them for weeks. The images were then rendered to confirm, and the harvest's page numbers proved to be **zero-based**, which is a trap its own tooling documents.
why:
**Sara Ruggiero gains an age, a birth year and a son.** Forty-five in 1817, so born about **1772**, and **still bearing children at forty-five** — a son, whose given name sits further down the act and was not reached. Andreana was born when her mother was about twenty-four. Two days ago this woman was a bracketed «[Rosae]» in a machine transcript. 

**And it opens a smaller question rather than closing everything.** Anna Falco married an Arcangelo Crisci on 3 May 1818, son of «*fu Nicola, e Chiara Majone*». The younger Arcangelo of strada Capodiconca was married to **Maria Martone** in 1817. Either he was widowed and remarried within months, or **there is a third man of the name**. Unresolved, and recorded as unresolved.

what: Pasqua Falco married — and a refusal this archive made on purpose is vindicated
was:
**PASQUA FALCO** has been one of this archive's oldest dead ends: «*absent from every searchable route*». Two women of the name sat in it, **both born about 1823**, and the archive **deliberately refused to join them**: 

**One** born 30 March 1823 to **Giuseppe Falco and Gelsomina Vigliotta** of strada Costa, found by reading the 1823 register end to end. **The other** the wife of **Francesco Arricale** of strada Capodiconca, twenty-five in December 1848 — **and the mother of GIOVANNA ARRICALE, generation five's wife.** Joining them would have attached the direct line to a documented household. The archive did not.
now:
**The refusal was right.** «*Num. d'ordine 29*», 9 September 1856: «*…**ANGELO MAJONE** … figlio di **Francesco Majone defunto** … e di **Marta Diglio defunta** … e **PASQUA FALCO, di anni TRENTATRÉ**, nata in Arienzo, figlia di **GIUSEPPE FALCO** … e di **GELSOMINA VIGLIOTTA defunta***». 

Thirty-three in 1856 is the child born 30 March 1823. **And she is not called a widow.** A woman who had married Francesco Arricale and borne him a daughter in 1848 would be *vedova* or still married in 1856; this act gives her as a spinster, with the standard documents list and no death act of a previous husband among them. 

**They are two women.** Generation five's grandmother is still unidentified, and the line is not attached to strada Costa.
how: Looking for Nunziata Falco. The work list asked whether **Giuseppe Nunzio and Nunziata** carry one family name, and the test was the marriage registers either side of 1855. Nunziata is in none of them — and 1856 turned out to carry **a filled alphabetical index bound at the front**, which listed «*29 Majone Angelo, e Pasqua Falco*» in one line.
why:
**This is what a deliberate refusal is for.** The archive could have joined the two Pasqua in a sentence and gained a generation; it wrote instead that the join was not established. An act read two weeks later says the join would have been false. 

**Three more facts fall out of the same two volumes.** Giuseppe Falco of strada Costa **remarried on 13 December 1854**, to Angela Carfora, and his act names **his own parents for the first time** — «*figlio del fu **FRANCESCO** … e della fu **MARIANGELA GIULIANI***» — and gives him as **VEDOVO DI GELSOMINA VIGLIOTTI**, living at **Santa Maria a Vico**. He was seventy-one, so born about 1783. 

**Gelsomina Vigliotta was dead before December 1854**, said twice, two years apart, in two acts read from the image. She should be in the Arienzo death registers for 1844–1858, which this archive has already read out — and she was not found there. That is now a question rather than a gap.

what: THE CORRECTIONS PAGE WAS AUDITED FOR THE FIRST TIME — nineteen entries in 187 were standing after the finding that overturned them
was: **This page has never been re-read.** It has been added to for a week — 187 entries, six of them explicitly headed WITHDRAWN — on the assumption that publishing a withdrawal is the same thing as retracting the claim. **Five withdrawals in two days is what made the assumption worth testing.**
now:
**Nineteen entries were still asserting something this archive had since overturned, and nothing on any of them said so.** Eleven of them are still labelled **open** and are not open: generation four's civil marriage act, hunted through sixty-four acts and «not where it has to be», was found at San Felice that afternoon; the Sant'Agnese parish «open question again» was settled by the act the same night; the founders' death window «that the arithmetic stops» was closed by the act itself; Filomena Annecchino's birthplace, doubted twice, is on this archive's own evidence; Pasqua Falco's birth, «every route tried and closed», was read out of the 1823 register two days later.

**The structural reason is on this page in plain sight.** The withdrawal is published as a **new entry at the top**, and the page sorts by date descending — so a withdrawal sits sixty entries away from the claim it kills, and a reader landing on the old one is told nothing. **The archive's rule is that corrections stay visible. It was keeping the correction visible and the supersession invisible.**
how: Reading all 187 entries end to end and cross-referencing every claim against later entries on the same subject — the fifteen marked `open` first, then every entry asserting an absence, then the three surnames known to collapse in this hand.
why:
**A correction that nobody can find from the thing it corrects is a note, not a correction** — which is the exact sentence this archive wrote about the Cioffi conflation three entries ago, about a household file. It applies to this page too.

**Each of the nineteen now carries the entry that replaced it**, named, dated and linked, at the top of its own text. **Nothing has been deleted or reworded.** The stale claim keeps its full text, struck through as before, with the supersession above it — because the failure is still the more useful half, and because an entry that was right for four hours and wrong after that is a more honest record of how this work goes than one that was never wrong.

**And the audit is now a recurring item on the work list**, because 187 entries took one pass and the page is still growing.
by: the first audit of this page

what: WITHDRAWN as a discovery — «1859 opened» was published the day before, from the same page of the same volume
was: Published here **today**: «*1859 carries its own alphabetical tavola, bound in at the front … it holds **three Falco deaths, none of them known here***», with **MARIA** and **RAFFAELE FALCO** «*di MICHELE, ed AMBROGIO MARIA GIOVANNA*» called «**a Falco household this archive has never recorded**» and «*No Ambrogio has ever appeared here as a Falco wife*».
now:
**All of it was published on 14 September**, from the same tavola: «*act 19, **FALCO MARIA**, contadina, of **Michele and d'Ambrogio Giovanna**, died 4 March; act 55, **FALCO CARMELA** … act 60, **FALCO RAFFAELE** … **No Vincenzo. 1859 is eliminated.***» 

**The household was not unrecorded — it was named, and so was what it had previously been known by**: «*Michele Falco × Maria Giovanna d'Ambrosio was known only by «a daughter Antonia born 19 November 1850»; it now has Maria and Raffaele.*» The «tavola bound at the front» note, the 1860 warning and the Michele/Michelangelo caution were all there too.
how: The audit of this page, cross-referencing entries on the same volume.
why:
**This is the sixth instance in one week of the same failure, and the first where the duplicate was of an entry on this very page.** The Nudgee graves were in three files when they were announced; the Cioffi correction was standing in the household file when it was re-broken; the deacon's death act was in the corrections log; the printed-year trap and the 1817 nil were both in `notes/`; the 1859 tavola was **here**.

**The pattern is no longer about which file was not read.** Five of the six were re-derived from a source this archive had already written, and the sixth from a source it had already published. **What is missing is not a habit of reading the notes. It is a check that runs before a finding is written up** — and the only one that would have caught this is the one that now exists: reading this page before adding to it.

**The substance stands.** 1859 really does hold those three deaths, the tavola really is at the front, and 1860 really has no index. The hours spent reading it a second time bought nothing.
by: the first audit of this page

what: FORTY VOLUMES OF MARRIAGE INDEXES WERE CLOSED AGAINST A SURNAME THIS ARCHIVE HAD RETIRED — the negative is void and the search is open again
was: Published here **today**, closing the largest sweep of the week: «*Every year from 1809 to 1849 has been read … **Maria Falco's marriage to Francesco COSSI is not in any of them.***» On that negative rested an argument that the couple married **before 1809**, that no index could ever hold them, and that **«the next instrument is the parish marriage register, not another index»**.
now:
**Her husband is FRANCESCO CIOFFI.** This archive corrected «Cossi» to «Cioffi» for the strada Camellara household months ago — «*Two different families, distinguished by the clerk and conflated by this archive*» — re-broke the correction this morning, and re-made it this afternoon at four times magnification, on the dot over the letter after the C.

**So forty volumes were read looking for the wrong man.** «Not in any of them» is a statement about the spelling COSSI. **It says nothing about whether a Falco × Cioffi marriage is in those indexes**, and the 1820s and 1830s volumes are sorted by surname, so an entry under CIOFFI would sit in a part of the page a searcher checking C-o-s was not reading closely.
how: The audit of this page: the withdrawal of «Giuseppa Cossi» and this negative carry the same date, and neither knew about the other.
why:
**The reading is not wasted and the conclusion is.** Every year from 1809 to 1849 really has been read and checked against its own tavola heading; 1836 really is absent from the series; the sideways filming of 1813 and 1829 is really recorded. **What is void is the one line the sweep was run to produce.**

**And the argument built on it is void with it.** «They married before the civil registers began» was inferred from an absence that was never tested, and it was about to send the next reader into the eighteenth-century parish register — the most expensive instrument this archive has — to look for a marriage that may be sitting in a volume already open on the desk.

**A negative is only as good as the string it was run on.** This archive already had an entry called «a negative produced by searching the wrong collection». This is the same failure one level down: the right collection, read completely, against a name it had itself retired. **The indexes are back on the work list, to be re-read for FALCO × CIOFFI.**
by: the first audit of this page

superseded.note: **Withdrawn within the hour.** The sweep was run on the **bride**, not the groom: the *What has been read* record lists year by year where **no FALCO married**, and reports thirteen Falco marriages found. what: A correction reopened — «Cioffi, not Cossi» was reversed at a resolution the entry itself says cannot tell them apart
was: On 13 September this archive corrected two declarants on strada Camellara **from CIOFFI to COSSI**: «*LUCA COSSI, 33, a SARTORE, and GIOVANNI COSSI, 43, a contadino — both of strada Camellara. **Cossi, not Cioffi.***»
now: **That correction is reopened, on the strength of its own reasoning.** Its method note reads: «*Cossi is short with a double-s; Cioffi is longer and carries the -ffi ligature. **At the resolution the plate was cropped to, they are not distinguishable.***» It then made the change anyway, at that resolution, and in the direction every later finding runs against — the strada Camellara family is **CIOFFI**, established twice.
how: The audit of this page, reading the entry's *how* against its *now*.
why:
**Two days later this archive settled how these shapes are separated, and it is not by length or by the double letter.** It is **the dot after the C for Cioffi, the round o for Cossi, the r for Crisci**, at eight times magnification — the test that caught «Anna Maria Cossi» as **CRISCI** and «Giuseppa Cossi» as **CIOFFI** in a single day.

**Neither reading is asserted here.** The two men may well be Cossi; strada Camellara held both families. What is not sound is a correction made at a resolution its own author recorded as insufficient. **It goes back on the work list to be re-rendered at 8× and read against the three-way test**, and until then the page it lives on should not be treated as settled in either direction.

what: THIS PAGE HAS BEEN PRINTING ITS OWN MARKUP FOR A WEEK — 151 entries published with their asterisks showing
was:
Every correction on this page is written in markdown, and the page printed the source. The live HTML reads «*`

`**VINCENZO FALCO and ANDREANA CRISCI** are the couple this whole line descends through*» — **with the asterisks in it**. 151 entries carried bold that never rendered, 60 carried backticked ark numbers that never became code, and every blank line between paragraphs collapsed into a space, so the arguments ran together in one block.
now: **Rendered.** The page now converts bold, inline code, links and paragraph breaks at build time, escaping the text first so the data file stays plain and untrusted markup cannot get through. Two entries that had smuggled in raw `<a href>` tags to get a working link — the only two that ever displayed correctly — are rewritten as ordinary markdown links.
how: The audit of this page. The fault was invisible from the source, which looks correct, and from the data, which is correct. It is only visible in the built HTML.
why:
**The emphasis on this page is not decoration.** These entries are arguments about evidence, and the bold is where the finding is — «**not one Falco appears in the 1817 births**», «**CIOFFI**», «**it was there**». Printing it as asterisks does not merely look unfinished; it flattens the one signal that tells a reader which clause is load-bearing.

**And it went unseen because nobody reads this page.** It is written to, daily, at length, and this audit is the first time anything has read it back — which is the same finding as the nineteen stale entries, arriving through a different door. **A page that is only ever appended to will drift in every way at once**: in what it claims, and in whether it renders.
by: the first audit of this page

what: WITHDRAWN within the hour — the forty volumes were not read against the wrong surname, and the audit that said so had not checked its own claim
was: Published here **an hour ago**, as the second finding of the first audit of this page: «*Forty volumes of marriage indexes were closed against a surname this archive had retired … **«Not in any of them» is a statement about the spelling COSSI.** It says nothing about whether a Falco × Cioffi marriage is in those indexes*». A work-list row was raised to re-read all forty, and the commit message said the conclusion built on the negative «*has nothing under it*».
now:
**The sweep was run on the BRIDE, and the bride's surname is not in doubt.** The record of it on the *What has been read* page lists, year by year, where **no FALCO married at Arienzo** — «*1809, 1810, 1811, 1812, 1815 … 1816, 1817, 1820, 1821, 1822, 1823, 1824, 1826, 1827…*» — and reports **thirteen Falco marriages found and published**, with five more Falco reached through the parents' column. **A reader working the F section of each tavola sees a Maria Falco whoever she is marrying.** The groom's surname never governed what was read.

**And this archive's own research note already had the surname right**, in the line naming what is still outstanding: «*the pre-1809 **Maria Falco × Francesco CIOFFI** marriage the civil series cannot hold*». **The negative stands, and so does the conclusion drawn from it:** every year from 1809 to 1819 is read out, the couple's son was five when he died in March 1824, and the Arienzo civil registers begin in 1809 — so the marriage is older than the series. **The parish register really is the next instrument.**
how: Reading `notes/QUEUE.md` and the *What has been read* entry for the sweep — which is what the withdrawn claim should have done before it was written.
why:
**The audit repeated the failure it had just finished describing, in the same hour, in the entry announcing it.** Two entries on this page carried the surname COSSI for a household corrected to CIOFFI; I inferred from the prose what the sweep had searched on, and did not open the page that records what it actually read. **A stale word in a sentence is not evidence that the work behind the sentence was stale.**

**What survives is small and real:** the prose of that entry and of the *What has been read* page names «Francesco COSSI» for a man this archive established is **Francesco CIOFFI**. That is a wrong name in a published negative, now fixed in both places. **It is a misspelling, not a void search**, and the work-list row raised to re-read forty volumes is struck rather than deleted, with this as the reason.

**The one thing the audit got right about itself was the timing.** This archive's rule is that a find is checked against what it already holds **in the same pass that publishes it**. That check ran an hour late, which is how this entry exists instead of a week of re-reading.
by: reading the notes the audit had just told everyone to read

what: CRESCENZO FALCO'S BIRTH DATE — 11 October 1819 — and the parish page that named him was already in this repository, unparsed
was: **CRESCENZO FALCO** has been in this archive as a name with two weddings and no beginning: a marriage of 3 February 1845, and a church act with «*dispensatione obtenta … super quarto gradu consanguinitatis … **Crescentium Falco, filium Josephi, e Antoniae di Guida***». **No birth, no age, no date of any kind.**
now:
**Arienzo, *Nati 1819*, act 99, folio 239, 11 October 1819**: «*è comparso **GIUSEPPE FALCO**, di anni **quaranta**, di professione **contadino**, domiciliato in questo comune, **strada Camellara** … ad ore cinque è nato nella sua propria casa da lui dichiarante, e da **ANTONIA DI GUIDA** sua moglie legitima d'anni **trentuno**, un **maschio***».

**The given name would not resolve in the civil hand** — not at the leaf's maximum resolution, which Antenati caps below the usual 3400 px for this image. So it was taken from somewhere else: the **parish** baptism page `3Q9M-CSD3-13CH-7`, an October 1819 entry «*et **Josepho Falco** et **Anto[nia] di [Guida]** Conjugibus*» with the marginal name «*Cresantios*» — the machine's rendering of **CRESCENTIUS**. **Two independent record series, the same parents, the same month.**
how: The 1819 birth register read act by act — 137 acts, six contact sheets — then the unreadable name checked against this archive's own parish harvest.
why:
**The parish page has been in this repository the whole time, with the child's column blank.** `data/falco-baptisms-parsed.tsv` carries the row — year 1819, father «Josepho Falco» — and the child was never parsed out of the mangled Latin, so nobody ever joined it to the Crescenzo who had no birth date three files away.

**This is the «harvesting is not holding» failure with the roles reversed, and that is what makes it worth writing down.** Every previous instance was a finding re-derived from scratch because nobody read the harvest. **Here the new work is what made the old harvest legible**: the civil act supplied the parents, the street and the month, and only then did a blank column in a TSV become a name. 

**A harvest is not a backlog of answers. It is a backlog of half-answers**, and the half it is missing is usually the one a second source supplies.
by: the 1819 birth register, read act by act

what: A CHILD NAMED FOR HIS BROTHER, THREE DAYS AFTER THE BURIAL — and a marriage found in the margin of his own birth act
was: This archive already held the worst day in the house of **Giuseppe Falco and Gelsomina Vigliotta**: on **15 March 1819** they buried **DOMENICO**, aged two years and four months, and **eleven hours later** his sister **ROSARIA**. Nothing was known of the household between that day and the birth of **Pasqua** in 1823.
now:
**Three days later a son was born and given the dead boy's name.** Arienzo, *Nati 1819*, **act 33, folio 206, 18 March 1819**, at half past seven in the morning: «*è comparso **GIUSEPPE FALCO** … di professione **massaro di campagna**, domiciliato in detto comune, **strada Camellara** … e da **GELSOMINA VIGLIOTTA** sua moglie legitima … un **maschio** … a cui si è dato il nome di **DOMENICO CLEMENTE***».

**And he lived.** Written later across the foot of his own birth act, in the registrar's hand: «*Con atto **6 agosto 1856** at[to] **21** in **S[anta] Maria a Vico** il Falco sposò **DOMENICA VIGLIOTTI** di Giuseppe*».
how: The 1819 birth register read act by act; the annotation magnified separately from the act.
why:
**Two things follow and the second is a new instrument.**

**The household is on STRADA CAMELLARA in 1819**, where this archive has it on **strada Costa** in 1816 — so either they moved, or the street does not identify this family. That matters, because **a second Giuseppe Falco declared a birth on the same street seven months later**, and he is a *contadino* married to *Antonia di Guida*. **Two men of one name on one street in one year**, separated only by trade and wife.

**And a birth act can carry a marriage.** The registrar's later cross-reference reached a wedding in **another comune** — one that no Arienzo marriage register would ever have shown. **This archive closed a question three days ago on exactly that shape**: Nunziata Falco is in none of the Arienzo marriage registers of 1854, 1855 or 1856, all read act by act. **If her birth act is found, its margin may hold what the registers do not.**
by: the 1819 birth register, read act by act

superseded.what: «SANTA MARIA A VICO» WAS MY GUESS, AND ITS OWN REGISTER EXCLUDES IT — the comune in the margin is not established
superseded.note: **«Santa Maria a Vico» was a guess and its own 1856 register excludes it** — act 21 there is Don Domenico de Lucia, promised 14 June, and there is no act of 6 August. The comune reads «S[?]basia a Vico» at five times and is **not established**. The bride's father reads **Gaspare**, not Giuseppe. **The marriage itself stands.**

what: Luigi Falco's CIVIL birth act — the day, the hour and both parents' ages behind a baptism already held
was: Generation three's son **LUIGI** was in this archive from the **parish** register alone: «*ex **Vincentio Falco**, ed **Andreana Crisci** … nominatus est **Aloysius***», dated only «**Dec 1819**».
now: **Act 133, 21 December 1819, at ten in the morning**: «*è comparso **VINCENZO FALCO**, di anni **ventisei**, di professione **contadino**, domiciliato in questo comune, **strada Camellara** … è nato nella sua propria casa da lui dichiarante e da **ANDREANA CRISCI** sua moglie legitima d'anni **ventidue**, un **maschio** … a cui si è dato il nome di **LUIGI***».
how: The 1819 birth register, read act by act. The act is fully legible at 3400 px — no reading in it is uncertain.
why:
**This is published as a confirmation, not a discovery, and the distinction was nearly lost.** The act was read as a new child for the direct line and written up as one. **The household file already held the baptism**, and the check that is supposed to run in the same pass as the publication caught it — **this time before the claim was made rather than two days after.**

**What is genuinely new is small and useful**: the exact day, the hour, the street, and both parents' stated ages. 

**And one of those ages is another demonstration.** Vincenzo Falco is **twenty-seven** on 10 May 1818 and **twenty-six** on 21 December 1819 — **a year younger after nineteen months.** His baptism of 1 February 1792 makes him twenty-seven here, so both civil figures are wrong. It is the fourth independent instance this week, and it is why this archive dates him from the font.
by: the check that runs in the same pass as the publication

what: THE CONTACT SHEET IS TRIAGE, NEVER A CLAIM — twice in one volume it gave me the reading I was hoping for
was: The 1819 birth register has **no annual tavola**, so its 137 acts were read through **six contact sheets**, each tiling twenty-four cropped bands at the line where the father's name, age, trade and street sit. It is the method that makes a 71-image volume affordable.
now:
**Twice in that one volume the sheet said what I wanted and the image said otherwise.**

A father read on the sheet as **«Alfonso Diglio … strada Camellara»** — the husband of the fourth Maria Falco, six years earlier than any sighting this archive has — is at magnification **«strada TERRA MURATA»**. Different street, and his wife is not a Falco either: the surname read as **«…Falco»** is **SILVIO** at eight times, with no F crossbar and an l-v-i-o where Falco has l-c-o.

**Both wrong readings were the ones that would have been findings.**
how: Magnifying each candidate before writing it down, which is this archive's standing rule for a hoped-for reading.
why:
**The sheet compresses a half-page into a strip about ninety pixels tall. That is enough to see that a word is not FALCO; it is not enough to see that it is.** The failure is asymmetric, and so the rule has to be: **a contact sheet may only ever produce a candidate, never a record.**

**It is the same rule that already governs this hand's three collapsing surnames** — Cossi, Crisci, Cioffi, separated only by the dot after the C, the round o and the r. The 1819 volume added a fourth trap of the same kind and a fifth: **a street name can be misread into a family.**

**And a control worth keeping.** Where a street carries a surname, the street checks the reading: act 22 of this year gives «*Francesco **Cossi** … strada **Cossi***», the same word twice in one sentence — which is how the strada Cossi family can be told from the strada Camellara **Cioffi** without any judgement at all.
by: magnifying every hoped-for reading

what: THE LIVING BRANCHES OF THIS FAMILY WERE DRAWN AS EMPTY BARS — the front page counted how much of each family was dead
was: The front page ranks the families who married in, grouped by how they reach this line. Under «*They carry this family's blood*» it drew **Crisci 15, Falcone 9, Biondo 5, Mazza 4, Zaino 2, Abatiello 1** — and then **eight more families with no bar at all**: **D'Arcy, Defranceski, Ellevsen, Halliday, Isla, Militano, Reid, Zavaglia.**
now:
**Those eight carry twenty-one of the fifty-one people of Falco blood, and every one of them is a LIVING branch.** 

The bar was never counting blood. It was plotting `n`, which `tools/build_marriedin.py` defines as `len(g["people"])` — **the people this archive can PUBLISH.** Living people are withheld by the rule that governs everything here, so they never reach that list, and a family whose descendants are all alive scored **zero**.

**And it failed in the other direction too.** **MAZZA** was drawn at **4** where only **two** of its people carry Falco blood; the other two are the dead kin its spouse came from, and the dead are the ones `n` counts. So the page said, of a house with two blood descendants and a house with two blood descendants, that the first had four and the second had none.

**The chart now plots the group's own count**, which `reachCount` has held all along: Crisci 10, Falcone 9, Biondo 7, Militano 6, Ellevsen 4, D'Arcy 3, Zavaglia 3, Defranceski 2, Mazza 2, and one each for Zaino, Abatiello, Halliday, Isla and Reid. **Fifty-one, every family visible, and the number means what the heading says.**
how: **David, reading his own front page: «*how can a Mazza carry Falco blood, but a D'Arcy or a Defranceski can't?*»** The classification was never wrong — `married-in.json` files both surnames under `blood` correctly. Only the bar was. **The question came from the one reader who could see the gap**, because the families drawn as nothing were his own.
why:
**The rule that protects living people turned this family's own living descendants into blank rows on its front page.** That is the whole finding, and it is the same shape as every other failure this archive has recorded this week: **a rule that is right about a person and wrong about a total.** The living-people rule is the most important one here and it was doing its job exactly as written — at the level of a person. Nobody had asked what it does to a sum.

**Nothing new is exposed by the fix.** The honest figure is an aggregate: how many people of a surname descend from a Falco. **That is strictly less than what this archive already publishes about living people** — their names, and who they married — under the name-and-relationship rule.

**The label went with it.** The chart described its own number as «*people this archive names*», which was the truthful name for the wrong figure and is a false one for the right figure. It now reads «*how many of their people reach this line*».

**And it was found by the only reader who would notice.** An archive can carry a fault like this indefinitely, because the families it renders as nothing are precisely the ones with nobody dead enough to write about — and so the page never looks empty to anyone but them.
by: David, reading the front page

what: CRESCENZO FALCO'S BIRTH DATE IS PROVEN — and his marriage act puts his mother alive twenty-five years later than anything this archive held
was: Six hours ago this archive gave **Crescenzo Falco** a birth date of **11 October 1819** and graded it **probable, not proven**, because the given name would not resolve in the civil hand — it was supplied by a parish page with the same parents and the same month. A work-list row asked for a third source before it was allowed to become proven.
now:
**Arienzo, *Matrimoni* 1845, act 3, folio 146, 2 February 1845**: «*sono comparsi nella Casa Comunale **CRESCENZO FALCO maggiore di anni VENTICINQUE, nato in ARIENZO**, di professione **colono** … figlio di **GIUSEPPE FALCO** … e di **ANTONIA DI GUIDA***».

**Twenty-five on 2 February 1845 puts his birth between 3 February 1819 and 2 February 1820.** The act of 11 October 1819 falls inside it. **Three sources — civil birth, parish baptism, civil marriage — one man.** The grading moves to proven.

**And the act gives his mother back.** «*ANTONIA DI GUIDA di professione **contadina** domiciliata **ivi***» — alive, with a trade and an address, **in an act that writes «DEFUNTO» for the bride's father and «DEFUNTA» for her mother in the very next sentence.**
how: The 1845 Arienzo marriage register, opened for the one act the work-list row named.
why:
**This archive held Antonia di Guida on ONE dated document** — her son's birth act of 11 October 1819, added this morning. Her death has been hunted through 229 Arienzo pages of the parish death register and not found. **Her window now opens on 2 February 1845 instead of October 1819: twenty-five years of her life restored by a document that was never about her.**

**The form is what makes it evidence.** This archive has a standing rule that the absence of «*fu*» proves nothing — three acts of one archpriest killed that inference. **This is a different instrument.** The clerk marked two parents dead in the same act, by name, and did not mark these two; and a dead parent does not get a profession and a domicile. **An absence inside a form that states the thing explicitly is not the same as an absence in prose.**

**Two smaller things.** Crescenzo is a **colono** on **strada Sant'Andrea**, and his father is «*di professione simile, domiciliato ivi*» — **so the household is off strada Camellara by 1845**, after twenty years of birth acts that place it there. And his bride **ANGELA MARIA MORGILLO** was an orphan of twenty-three; the church act's dispensation «*super quarto gradu consanguinitatis*» makes them third cousins, which is the fourth Falco marriage inside the fourth degree this archive has now documented.
by: the work-list row that refused to let a probable reading become proven

superseded.what: «ivi» means the comune and never the street — settled in two printed forms, and it costs this archive a published finding
superseded.note: **PARTLY WITHDRAWN.** The finding stands; one sentence in it does not. Crescenzo's birth date is still proven and Antonia di Guida is still alive on 2 February 1845 — that turns on the form marking two other parents dead and not these two, and nothing here touches it. **But «*so the household is off strada Camellara by 1845*» rested on the word «ivi», and «ivi» is the comune.** The act places the father at Arienzo and gives no street at all. **The household may never have left.**

what: WITHDRAWN — «Cossi, not Cioffi» was wrong in one direction and right in the other, and the data file had the better half all along
was: On 13 September this archive corrected two declarants on Chiara Rivetti's death act **from CIOFFI to COSSI**: «*LUCA COSSI, **33**, a SARTORE, and GIOVANNI COSSI, **43**, a contadino — both of strada Camellara. **Cossi, not Cioffi.***» The audit of this page reopened it yesterday, because its own method note says that at the resolution used «*they are not distinguishable*».
now:
**Read at magnification: the surname is CIOFFI.** Arienzo *Morti 1843*, `an_ua14345`, atto 43, image 30R: «*sono comparsi **LUCA CIOFFI** di anni **trentatré**, di professione **Sartore**, regnicolo, domiciliato in **strada Camellara**, e **GIOVANNI CIOFFI** di anni **quarantatré**, di professione **contadino**, regnicolo, domiciliato in **strada Camellara***».

**The test is the ligature, and it is unambiguous at this size.** Both words carry **two tall ascenders joined, with a long descender loop** — the *ff*. This archive's own note for the withdrawn correction described the difference exactly right and then read it backwards: «*Cossi is short with a double-s; Cioffi is longer and carries the -ffi ligature*». These words are the long ones.

**But the ages in the withdrawn correction were right, and the data file's were not.** `households.json` has carried «*Giovanni Cioffi, **48***» since it was written. The act says **forty-three**.
how: Row 28 of the work list, which the audit of this page raised: re-render at magnification and apply the three-way test — the dot after the C, the round o, the r.
why:
**Two records of one act, each holding half the truth, disagreeing for two days and never compared.** The corrections page had the ages right and the surname wrong. The household file had the surname right and an age wrong. **Neither was checked against the other**, and the page that exists to record this archive's mistakes was itself the one carrying the wrong name.

**The withdrawn correction was made at a resolution its own author recorded as insufficient**, and in the direction every later finding runs against — the strada Camellara family is CIOFFI, established twice more since. **That is the lesson worth keeping: a correction that admits it cannot see the evidence is not a correction, it is a coin toss with a citation.**

**Both errors are now fixed, in both files**, and the age is corrected visibly in the household record rather than swapped.
by: work-list row 28, raised by the audit of this page

what: EIGHT CITATIONS POINTED AT THE WRONG PAGE — every birth act copied out of an early note is off by one, and nobody had ever followed one back
was: This archive cites its birth acts by volume, image and act: «*ANTENATI `an_ua14415` img**41r** act47*» for **RAFFAELE FALCO, generation four**, born 10 May 1818. **Eight household records carried a citation of that form** — four in the 1816 volume, one in 1817, three in 1818.
now:
**Not one of them resolves.** Image 41r of the 1818 volume is a child called **Angelo**; Raffaele's act is on image **42**. Image 29l of 1816 is a Martone; Raffaele of 1816 is on **30**. Image 46r of 1818 is a **Sanzone** at folio 153; Maddalena Falco is on **47**. Image 59l of 1816, 35l of 1817 — **every one is one page early, and all six tested shifted by exactly one.**

**The cause is a numbering system, not a slip.** These citations were copied out of `notes/1818-birth-register-progress.md` and its siblings, which were written from a **harvest whose page numbers are ZERO-BASED**. This archive already knew that — it is written down for `data/sweep-people.tsv` — and the note's numbers went into the data file unconverted anyway.

**All eight are corrected and each now carries why**, rather than being quietly renumbered.
how: Work-list row 46, which was about something else entirely: sweeping the MARGINS of birth acts already held, for the marriage annotations found yesterday. **The first act opened was not the act the citation named**, and the row turned into this.
why:
**A citation nobody follows is decoration.** These eight have been on the site through every audit this archive has run — the corrections audit, the link checker, the release gate — because **not one of those tools opens an image.** `checkarchive` verifies that every internal link resolves to a page that exists. Nothing verifies that a citation resolves to the act it claims.

**The deaths are sound, and that is the part worth keeping.** The Arienzo death-register citations were spot-checked and they land exactly right — Chiara Rivetti's act of 1843 is at `an_ua14345` img30r, as cited. **Those notes were written with `tools/antenati.py`, which is one-based; the birth notes were written from the harvest, which is not.** The archive has been running two numbering systems and citing both in the same field.

**One thing fell out of the fix.** Read side by side, the two corrected 1816–18 acts separate the two Giuseppe Falco cleanly: **25 November 1816, Giuseppe Falco, 36, *massaro*, strada COSTA, wife GELSOMINA VIGLIOTTA, 32**; **7 June 1818, Giuseppe Falco, 36, *contadino*, strada CAMELLARA, wife ANTONIA DI GUIDA, 30.** The same stated age, nineteen months apart, on two different streets with two different wives — which is the documentary basis for a separation this archive had been making on other grounds.
by: work-list row 46, which was looking for something else

what: THE MARKDOWN FAULT WAS ON TWENTY-FOUR PAGES, NOT ONE — and the page that had already solved the living-people problem was the page the front page then broke
was: Yesterday this archive found that **/corrections/ had been publishing its own asterisks for a week** and fixed it — in that page. Three work-list rows asked the obvious follow-up questions: **is it anywhere else, is the living-people zero anywhere else, and does /marriages/ share the chart's defect?**
now:
**The markdown fault was on twenty-three more pages.** The built HTML — the only place it shows — carried literal markup on **/worklist** (60 backticks), **/register** (34), **/searched** (28), **/households** and **/people/crescenzo-falco** (13 unrendered bold each), and **nineteen /who/ pages** printing a plate filename in backticks. It is fixed by **one renderer instead of five**: `site/src/lib/md.js`, with /corrections/ moved off its private copy onto the shared one. **/worklist is the exception** — its component is the shared kit's, and the bug is reported rather than patched.

**The living-people zero was NOT anywhere else, and the reason is worth stating.** Every other total on this site is drawn from a population: the front-page Numbers count `people.json`, which holds **all 106 living people** with pages of their own. **The chart was the one total built from a field that means «publishable».**

**And /marriages/ does not share the defect — it solved it first.** That page buckets families three ways and gives the third its own name: **`held`, where `n === 0`**, rendered with a withheld count and the sentence «*Where a family appears with **no named people at all**, every person the archive holds for that surname is living.*»
how: Work-list rows 52, 53 and 54, raised by the audit of the corrections page. Row 53 was answered by grepping the BUILT HTML with tags stripped, which is the only view in which the fault is visible at all.
why:
**The most useful of the three answers is the one that found nothing.** `/marriages/` had already worked out what to do about a family with no publishable people, and said so in plain words on the page. **The shared rule was then extracted into `marriedin.js` precisely so the two pages could not drift** — and the chart drifted anyway, because it took the filing and left behind the treatment of zero, which was never in the lib to take.

**Extracting a rule moves the rule. It does not move the knowledge around the rule**, and the knowledge is usually the part that took the work. That is worth more than the bug it explains, because this estate is in the middle of extracting a great many rules into a shared kit.

**One thing found in passing:** `/families/` carried `***a kinsman***` typed straight into the template — an author's slip, not a rendering fault, and invisible for exactly as long.
by: three work-list rows raised by an audit

what: PASQUA FALCO MARRIED TWICE — the second wedding was written in the margin of her own birth act, fifty-seven years later
was: Pasqua Falco was this archive's oldest dead end until yesterday, when her marriage to **ANGELO MAJONE on 9 September 1856** was found and, because she was **not called a widow**, vindicated a refusal this archive had made on purpose. **After 1856 she disappeared again.**
now:
**Arienzo, *Nati 1823*, act 38 — her own birth act — carries this across its foot:** «*A **30 Dic.re 1880** l'Uf.le dello Stato Civile d'**Arienzo** sposò **PASQUA FALCO** con **PASQUALE CARFORA*** — 27 Agosto 1881».

**She married again at fifty-seven**, and on the ordinary reading as Angelo Majone's widow. The identification needs no argument: the annotation is physically on act 38, «*il nome di **PASQUA***», born 30 March 1823 to Giuseppe Falco — **the same act the 1856 marriage pointed to when it gave her age as thirty-three.**
how: Work-list row 46 — sweeping the margins of birth acts already held. Her act was opened because she married after 1855, which is where the pattern below said to look.
why:
**CARFORA is a name this archive hunts, and this is not it.** Maria Carfora of Forchia is generation seven's grandmother and her parents are unreachable through three closed routes. **Pasquale Carfora of this act is NOT claimed as kin to her** — the surname is dense at Forchia and present at Arienzo, and nothing whatever joins the two. **It is recorded because the next reader will notice the name and should find the refusal already written down.**

**What is now reachable:** the Arienzo civil marriage register for **30 December 1880**, which would name Pasquale Carfora's parents and state Pasqua as *vedova di Angelo Majone* — confirming the chain from a second document rather than from an annotation.

**And a marginal note is a marriage nobody would otherwise look for.** This one is fifty-seven years downstream of the page it is written on. No index reaches it, no search returns it, and it was found by opening a document this archive had already read.
by: the margin of an act this archive had already read

what: «Luigi Falco's blank margin is a real negative» — corrected within the hour, and the instrument turns out to have a date
was: Published on the work list an hour ago: **LUIGI FALCO's birth act of 21 December 1819 carries no marginal annotation**, where Domenico Clemente Falco's carries his 1856 marriage — «*That is a real negative for row 41*», the row that asks where Luigi's marriage is.
now:
**It was not a negative, because the control had not been run.** Two acts whose marriages are certain were then opened, and **both are blank**: **RAFFAELE FALCO**, generation four, born 10 May 1818 and married 5 March 1844 — nothing; **CRESCENZO FALCO**, born 11 October 1819 and married 2 February 1845 — nothing.

**But the four acts make a pattern, and it is not «sporadic».** Sorted by the date of the MARRIAGE rather than the volume:

**1844 Raffaele — no annotation. 1845 Crescenzo — no annotation. 1856 Domenico Clemente — annotated. 1880 Pasqua — annotated.**

**The birth volumes span 1818 to 1823 and do not predict it. The marriage dates do.** On four points the practice appears to begin somewhere between 1845 and 1856.
how: Running the control that should have been run before the negative was published — an act whose marriage is already known.
why:
**A negative from an instrument nobody has calibrated is not a negative.** An hour separated the claim from its refutation, and the only reason it was an hour is that the control was cheap; it should have been run first, and this archive has a standing rule saying so.

**What survives is better than what was claimed.** Luigi's blank no longer means «he did not marry». It means **he did not marry after about 1855 anywhere that notified Arienzo** — which is a bounded negative rather than a null, and it leaves 1840–1855 wide open. His death in 1864 at forty-five still wants explaining.

**And the pattern makes the instrument predictable.** Four points is a hypothesis, not a law, and it is written here as one. But it says where to spend the next render: **on the birth acts of people who married after 1855.** **NUNZIATA FALCO married on 13 November 1855** — exactly on the boundary — which is now the most interesting margin in the archive rather than a hopeful one.
by: the control that should have run first

what: The list at the back of the birth volumes is not what it looked like — and it names generation four
was: Reading 1819 end to end, this archive found **a twenty-one row list on the last leaf** — parents' names and birth dates, scattered across the year, headed «*Nomi, e cognomi de' genitori*» — and noted that **if it were a list of births declared late or out of series, it would explain acts that were never drawn.** That mattered: **ROSARIA FALCO** died on 15 March 1819 and her birth act is in none of 1816, 1817, 1818 or 1819.
now:
**The same list is at the back of 1818, and it includes a birth that is in the main register.** Row two reads «*[Vince]nzo **FALCO** ed Andreana **CRISCI** — **10 Maggio 1818***» — **Raffaele Falco, generation four**, act 47, folio 149, sitting at image 42R where it always was.

**So it is not a register of the missing, and it cannot explain Rosaria.** What it is remains unsettled: the «Osservazioni» column carries a roman numeral (**VIII** in 1818, **XI** in 1819) and it faces the Procuratore del Re's 1849 certificate about counting the sheets and removing the blank ones, which suggests a reconciliation of renumbered folios. **That is a guess and is published as one.**
how: Opening the last leaf of the 1818 volume to see whether the 1819 list recurs. It does.
why:
